articles.title: Feminist activist Gloria Steinem dies at age 92
articles.summary: The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women

blocks.text: WOMEN'S RIGHTS. Gloria Steinem protests against the opening of the first United States branch of De Beers jewelry store in New York, on June 22, 2005.
Keith Bedford/Reuters
The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women

items: Gloria Steinem, a prominent American feminist writer and activist, passed away at the age of 92, leaving behind a legacy of fighting for gender equality and women's rights for over five decades.

She co-founded Ms. Magazine and was instrumental in the feminist movement, advocating for issues such as abortion rights, equal pay, and domestic violence, while also emphasizing the importance of listening to women's stories.

Steinem received numerous accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and continued her activism and writing well into her 80s, influencing generations of women and shaping the discourse on feminism.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Gloria Steinem, the American writer, lecturer, activist, and organizer who fought for gender equality and women’s civil and reproductive rights for more than five decades, has died, her foundation said. She was 92 years old.
The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women.
She died on Wednesday, September 2, her foundation said in an Instagram post on Thursday, September 3.

“From reluctant spokesperson to a beacon of positive change, hers is a singular journey — an American leader who can speak to us all,” film and theater director Julie Taymor said of Steinem in a 2017 New York Times interview.

Taymor directed the 2020 film “The Glorias,” depicting Steinem’s life across the years and based on her 2015 best-selling autobiography “My Life on the Road.” She was also the subject of a 2018 play, “Gloria: A Life,” and a 2011 HBO documentary, “Gloria: In Her Own Words.”
Steinem said she considered herself “an entrepreneur of social change.”

“I want to do justice to the women I meet, to tell their stories,” she told the New Yorker magazine in 2015. “It’s making connections, and using myself to listen, because we can’t empower women without listening to their stories.”

Steinem founded the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 with former US Representatives Bella Abzug and Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan, whose 1963 book “The Feminine Mystique” ushered in the second wave of feminism.
Among other groups, she also created the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Women’s Media Center, Voters for Choice, and the Ms. Foundation for Women.
In 2013, then-president Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest US civilian honor.

With her signature long, blonde-streaked, center-parted hair and aviator glasses, Steinem was the glamorous, hip symbol of the feminist movement, which she emphasized should embrace women of every race.
“If you’ve suffered discrimination, you’re sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of color basically invented feminism,” she told the New Yorker.

Steinem was born on March 25, 1934, in Toledo, Ohio, the younger of two daughters. Her father was a traveling antique dealer. Because the family moved frequently she did not attend school regularly until about seventh grade.
Her parents separated when she was 11, following which Steinem lived with and took care of her mother, who had a mental breakdown and suffered from depression.
The experience impacted Steinem’s views on social injustice and marriage, which she believed robbed women of choices and many of their civil rights.
“I’d already been the very small parent of a very big child, my mother. I didn’t want to end up taking care of someone else,” she was quoted as saying.
After graduating from Smith College, Steinem began freelancing as a journalist.

In 1963, she worked as a Playboy bunny for 11 days for a story for Show magazine. Her two-part groundbreaking expose, “A Bunny’s Tale,” detailed the poor pay and sexist treatment Playboy bunnies — originally waitstaff — endured. The story was made into a 1985 TV movie starring Kirstie Alley.
In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where her essay titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation” established her as a feminist leader at a time of roiling social change.

But it wasn’t until she attended an abortion speak-out in a New York church the following year that Steinem — who had had a then-illegal abortion in London when she was 22 — said her life as a feminist activist really began.

Ms. Magazine, which she co-founded in 1971, tackled abortion and other issues such as sexism, equal pay, and domestic violence — a far cry from the diet of beauty, cookery and supporting-your-husband topics that were the staple of magazines aimed at women.

An early issue included the names of 52 women, including Steinem, who had had abortions, and called for the procedure to be legalized ahead of the landmark 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling that recognized women’s constitutional right to abortion in the US for nearly half a century.
Steinem was often critical of the limitations of marriage. “Women are not going to be equal outside the home until men are equal in it,” she said.
She had no children of her own, and it was not until she turned 66 that she decided to wed — to South African businessman and environmentalist David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.

“I hope this proves what feminists have always said — that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives,” she said in a statement about the marriage. David Bale died of brain cancer in 2003.

Steinem continued working into her 80s. She wrote numerous books, including 1986’s “Marilyn: Norma Jean” about Marilyn Monroe, “Revolution from Within: A Book of Self-Esteem” about personal development, and books of essays.

She narrated and conceived the idea for an Emmy Award-winning documentary about child abuse, “Multiple Personalities: The Search for Deadly Memories,” for HBO in 1993 and produced the Lifetime film “Better Off Dead.” She also hosted “Woman,” a documentary series about violence against women, for the Viceland TV channel.

Author Carolyn Heilbrun — who penned 1995 biography “Education of a Woman: The Life of Gloria Steinem” — described her as “the epitome of female beauty and the quintessence of female revolution.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: John Lewis to launch YouTube chatshow to improve AI search results
articles.summary: Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon

blocks.text: John Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results.

The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air on YouTube with clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast.

blocks.caption: Angela Scanlon will host the Gift List ‘vodcast’.  Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show. There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off.

Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which is forcing retailers to change their marketing plans.

The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology.

Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its ‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge.
Ruis, who departs John Lewis this weekend after almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”.
He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.

Ruis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas.

Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend.

The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said.
“It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.”
after newsletter promotion
Ruis last month announced his abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”.
He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry.

“We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”.

Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which was bought out of administration by Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month.
He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.

articles.title: Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
articles.summary: The US vice-president recently mused with a Christian podcast host on whether the end of the world was nigh.

blocks.text: Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.

Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.

His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."
In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.
In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.
Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.
Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.

"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.
"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."
The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."
But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."
Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."
He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.

Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.
Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.
Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.
Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

articles.title: Teenager in Wales given detention sentence for stabbing teacher in head
articles.summary:
Judge voices concern about possible copycat incidents after boy, 16, found guilty over attack at school in Pembrokeshire

A judge has expressed concern over possible copycat attacks on school…

blocks.text: A judge has expressed concern over possible copycat attacks on school staff as he sentenced a teenager who stabbed a teacher in the head to four and a half years in youth detention.
Judge Thomas KC said it was the second such attack in south-west Wales in two years and that the authorities might have to consider what security measures were in place to protect teachers.

The boy, who was 15 at the time of the attack, approached the history teacher Vicki Williams when she was alone in a classroom at Milford Haven comprehensive school in Pembrokeshire, and asked her to check his work.
He shut the door of the classroom, pulled out a kitchen knife with a 20cm (8in) blade and attacked Williams. She managed to grab the knife from him and he fled.
Williams sustained a wound to her scalp, scratches on her back and minor cuts to her hands.
Christopher Rees KC, prosecuting, told Swansea crown court the attack in February had been “carefully planned” and that the boy had waited until the teacher was alone.
The boy, who is now 16 and cannot be named, was found guilty by a jury of wounding Williams with intent.
Williams told the court she thought she was going to die and expressed anger that her young daughter could have been left without a mother.
In victim personal statements she said she had been unable to return to teaching and was suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder.
She said she always kept the doors of her home locked, had installed security cameras there and had not been able to be left alone in the weeks after the attack.
Williams said she felt guilty she had not been able to return to work and help her students and colleagues.

She said she was nervous around young men and scared to go to the area where her attacker lived. “I don’t think I could be the same teacher I was before,” she said. If someone asked her for help, she feared she would “freak out”.

Thomas said the boy had not said why he attacked Williams but that it might have been that she had upset him in some way. The judge also said he was part of a group of boys “winding each other up to do stupid things to teachers”.
Thomas added: “You are much bigger and stronger than she is and you knew that.” He told the boy: “You could have killed her.”
In April 2024 a schoolgirl attempted to murder two teachers and a pupil by stabbing them with a blade at a school in Carmarthenshire, south-west Wales. She was detained for 15 years.
Thomas said: “I have concerns there may have been here or will in the future be a copycat element,” and that the authorities needed to be aware of this when considering security measures.
He told the boy: “I want anyone who is ever thinking in the future of doing the same to know what will happen to them if they do.

“They will spend a lot of their teenage years and perhaps beyond unable to go out with their friends, go and do what they want, go on holidays, have fun, be with their parents, follow their hobbies, and do what the rest of their friends are doing.”

articles.title: MILF chair turns emotional during assembly in Maguindanao del Norte
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY — Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim became visibly emotional during the speech of MILF commander Abdullah “Commander Bravo” Macapaar. The moment…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY — Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim became visibly emotional during the speech of MILF commander Abdullah “Commander Bravo” Macapaar.
The moment took place at the MILF-Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF) general assembly in Camp Darapanan, Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte on Thursday, Sept. 3.
In his speech, Macapaar reaffirmed his loyalty to Ebrahim and the MILF leadership in the face of internal tension that created divisions within their ranks.

Macapaar, a member of Bangsamoro Transition Authority, emphasized unity and loyalty to the MILF leadership and their principles, including the transition from armed struggle to peaceful political and democratic means.
“My loyalty to our Ameer (commander), Kagi Murad, is non-negotiable. My loyalty to the MILF is forever,” Macapaar said in Maranao language translated for the Inquirer by an MILF official.
While Macapaar was speaking, Ebrahim was seen shedding tears along with other MILF officials on stage.
Macapaar recalled how they fought together government forces in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao to defend their camps and their desire for Moro self-rule.
He narrated about ultimate sacrifices of muhajideen (fighters) and comrades being killed by bullets from government forces right before his eyes.

In August 2008, following the botched signing of the Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain (MOA-AD) between the government and the MILF, Bravo led MILF forces in attacking coastal villages in Kauswagan and Kolambugan towns in Lanao del Norte. /apl

articles.title: Habagat to bring heavy rains over Luzon, Visayas through Saturday
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to bring rains over Luzon and Visayas until Saturday, Sept. 5, the state weather bureau said. According to the Philippine…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to bring rains over Luzon and Visayas until Saturday, Sept. 5, the state weather bureau said.

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), Occidental Mindoro may experience up to 200 millimeters (mm) of rainfall on Friday until Saturday.
Pagasa warned of floods and landslides that may occur during severe weather conditions.
It also forecast 50 to 100 mm of rainfall over the following areas:

items: Tarlac
Zambales
Pampanga
Bataan
Bulacan
Metro Manila
Cavite
Batangas
Oriental Mindoro

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Visayas and the rest of Luzon may experience cloudy skies with isolated rain showers due to the enhanced habagat.
Mindanao, may have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with localized thunderstorms.

Pagasa weather specialist John Manalo said in the 5 p.m. weather advisory that the southwest monsoon will continue to bring moderate to occasional heavy rains over the country due to the enhancement of Tropical Storm Krovanh, formerly Pilandok.
Pilandok exited the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) early around 4 a.m. Thursday.
“At kahit lumabas na ito ng PAR kaya gusto natin ito banggitin dahil meron pa rin itong enhancement na ginagawa, partly, pinapalakas nito ang hanging habagat,” Manalo said.
(“And even though it has already left the PAR, we want to mention it because it still has some enhancement going on, partly, it is strengthening the southwesterly winds,”)/dp

articles.title: Alarm as US domestic violence killings remain high despite drop in homicides
articles.summary:
Non-profits say requests for legal help and housing on rise amid Trump funding cuts for prevention and response

As cities and states across the US report historic drops in homicides,…

blocks.text: As cities and states across the US report historic drops in homicides, domestic violence killings remain alarmingly high.

In Chicago, where homicides fell from 805 in 2021 to 425 in 2025, killings tied to domestic violence increased by 15% between 2024 and 2025. In Kansas City, Missouri, homicides in general have dropped since 2023, but 2025 was the second deadliest year for homicides tied to domestic violence. In Ohio, too, 2025 was the deadliest year for domestic violence killings, while homicides in general followed the national decrease. Across the US, the share of violent crimes that involve domestic violence has increased from 25% in 2020 to 27.5% in 2024, according to a 2026 FBI report.

Sometimes the killings make national headlines, like in April, when eight children were killed and two women were injured in Shreveport, Louisiana, or when several people were murdered in rural Oregon and in Billings, Montana, last month.

But national non-profit groups say they are receiving calls daily from people who are at high risk of being killed by their intimate partner. They are also hearing more from people seeking housing or legal help, they say.

“The number one need articulated over and over again is housing, and number two is legal support,” said Nikhita Ved, chief programs officer for the National Domestic Violence Hotline. “The folks that reach out might have had a family member who was killed or are people who fear they will be killed by their intimate partner, or they’re seeing severe signs.”
In 2020, the hotline received nearly 637,000 calls. In 2025, it answered a million, according to their data.

Though it’s nearly impossible to pinpoint a single cause for stubbornly high rates of domestic violence homicides in pockets of the US, the resources to prevent such tragedies are well-known, Ved adds. Still, they are not funded at a level that matches the scale of need.

The concerns about funding have only increased during the second Trump administration. Early into Trump’s second presidency, administration officials cut hundreds of millions in grants from research institutions, and domestic violence prevention and response non-profits that serve people of color, LGBTQ+ people and people with disabilities. In the notices to the affected groups, the federal government said their grants were being terminated because their work no longer aligns with the administration’s goals.

Some of those grants, like those for pet-friendly domestic violence shelters and domestic violence hotlines, were ultimately restored. But the National Network to End Domestic Violence warns that Trump’s proposed 2027 budget includes a nearly $30m reduction in funding for grant programs for transitional housing and legal assistance.
“Cuts are always devastating, because this work, it’s always been underfunded,” Ved said.

“There’s a diminishing in resources and in groups knowing if they can continue their work,” echoed Anita Raj, executive director of the Newcomb Institute and a professor of public health at Tulane University in New Orleans.

“Non-profits are having to decrease their workforce, which is a grave concern in Louisiana,” she adds. “We’re not a wealthy state, and our ability to backstop funding that’s been lost has a really chilling effect on the ability that we have to provide resources.”

When the president spoke out about the issue, he described “the scourge of domestic violence” as a criminal issue that he plans to address through deportations and going after human-trafficking rings. Raj said that this framing obscured the risk factors that most commonly lead to a homicide, like stalking, controlling behavior and threats to harm their partner or themselves. All of which have nothing to do with someone’s immigration status.

“Stop focusing on a demographic profile and focus on a behavioral profile,” Raj said. “[Intimate partner violence and homicides] problems that are not just as simple as a criminal justice issue and it’s not going to be improved by immigration enforcement,” she said.

When asked about the increase in domestic violence homicides and concerns about the 2027 budget’s impact on domestic violence, the White House referred the Guardian to its office of management and budget (OMB). The OMB did not respond to questions.

Raj warns that though tragedies like the recent killings in Louisiana, Oregon and Montana receive a lot of media attention, they are just the tip of the iceberg. She hopes to see more lawmakers and journalists talk about early signs of abuse, which can range from using fear and threats of violence to control a partner to hitting and choking. She also wants to see more education for young people about conflict resolution and healthy relationships, especially those who are growing up in homes where they are witnessing domestic violence.
“The danger of [this focus], is that it’s the tip of the iceberg and are the most extreme cases of something that’s so ubiquitous,” Raj said.

articles.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border

blocks.text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

blocks.caption: A protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta. Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

blocks.caption: People who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.  Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPA

blocks.text: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.
Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

articles.title: Can Hichilema heal Zambia's political divide?
articles.summary: The Zambian president starts a second term after a contested election exposed deep political divisions. His challenge now is to unite the country while addressing concerns over political freedoms.

image.caption: Hichilema was sworn in at an event at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital Lusaka in front of thousands of supportersImage: Jean Mandela/REUTERS

blocks.text: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for a second five-year term on Tuesday.

For decades, Zambia has worn its peaceful transfers of power almost like a badge of honor in a region where elections have too often ended in disputed results, violence or leaders refusing to leave. Hichilema's own victory in 2021 appeared to strengthen that reputation.
Five years later, the picture is more complicated.

Hichilema begins his second term after a disputed election, with his main challenger facing treason charges, opposition supporters questioning the credibility of the vote and controversy surrounding the closure of courts during the crucial window for election petitions.

Hichilema has promised reconciliation. But for a president who once sat on the other side of power as an opposition leader and treason suspect himself, the test now is whether those words will be matched by the political space he gives his opponents.
Ngobola Cengelo Muyembe, a political, business and social analyst, told DW that reconciliation must begin by recognizing that a significant part of the electorate backed someone else.

"You have to remember that in every 10 people that voted, four people voted for the other side," Muyembe said, noting that during the president's inaugural address, he spoke about reconciliation and uniting people. "But that message can only resonate if what is on the ground reflects what is being spoken about."
Can Hichilema reunite a divided country?

Raymond, a self-employed Zambian who asked that his full name not be used, told DW that Hichilema should look beyond who supported him at the ballot box and govern across Zambia's political and ethnic divisions.

"The president, congratulations! Don't think about people who voted for you, didn't vote for you. One Zambia, one nation, one city," Raymond said. "Real change in mines and agriculture. The mines want us Zambians to be benefiting. Even your Tonga, your Bemba, you are all Zambians."

blocks.caption: The southern African nation has held largely peaceful elections since it returned to multiparty democracy in 1991Image: Jean Mandela/REUTERS

blocks.text: Artist Mazuba Nzabuka told DW he also wants Hichilema to govern those who supported him and those who did not, while giving young people a greater voice.

"Going forward, he is going to do the promises left behind. He is a president for all people," said Nzabuka. "Those who did not vote for him, those who voted for him. We are the same people. The five years going forward, our voices can be heard. Look after the youths."
But reconciliation will have to contend with the political fallout from the election.

Zambia returned to multiparty democracy in 1991 and has since witnessed several changes of governing parties through elections. Hichilema himself benefited from that tradition when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu in 2021.
The latest election prompted debate about whether that image remains intact.
Democracy faces a new test
The independence of Zambia's institutions may feature prominently during Hichilema's second term.

Critics said their concerns intensified after courts were closed on the final day available for presidential election petitions. Interruptions during the announcement of election results prompted some opposition supporters to question the process.
Can Zambia trust election referee?
Analyst Muyembe said that protecting political speech and allowing opponents to openly challenge the government will be crucial to rebuilding confidence.

"If you really respect the people that voted against you, allow them to speak, engage them in a debate, not where you just have to bring in only the people that agree with you and the ones that are talking to themselves on TV, and encourage this national dialogue," Muyembe told DW.

"Allow the opposition who lost to complain about it the way they want, and then from there you can chart a way forward. But to stifle debate and fudge facts, this is not really helping our democracy."

The arrest of Hichilema's main challenger, Brian Mundubile, and his running mate on treason charges linked to allegations of plotting an armed uprising has become another point of political controversy.
Authorities maintain that the case concerns national security, while opposition supporters have questioned the timing of the arrests.
The situation has drawn attention because Hichilema himself once faced a treason charge while in opposition.

The question of whether the institutions that once wielded enormous power over him can operate independently when dealing with his own political opponents is likely to remain part of the debate surrounding his second term.
From economic stability to household relief
Political freedoms are not the only test.
Hichilema enters his second term pointing to progress in stabilizing Zambia's economy, including lower inflation and the restructuring of the country's external debt.
But many Zambians are waiting for those gains to reach their homes.
Mutinta Mushabati, who attended the inauguration at Heroes Stadium in the capital Lusaka, told DW that she was encouraged by what she heard from Hichilema.

"That he is going to increase everything, new allowances for school-going children, social cash transfer, CDF," she said, refering to Zambia's expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.
"I'm very excited right now. I don't even know what I can say. I'm very happy."
Muyembe told DW that the gap between positive national economic indicators and the experience of ordinary households represents a key challenge for Hichilema's second term.
He compared the economy to a reservoir that may be full while the pipes carrying water to individual homes remain blocked.
"Imagine that you got a giant command reservoir that distributes water to houses in the village," the analyst said.

"When the reservoir is full, you have stabilized your macroeconomic arrangement. But if the pipes that take water to the small little villages, the small little houses in these villages, are clogged and blocked, then you haven't really solved the issue because the people need to have the water in their individual houses."
Making Zambia's minerals work for Zambians
Copper and mining remain central to Zambia's economy and could provide one route for translating economic growth into household gains.

Muyembe told DW that Hichilema's government should focus not simply on attracting billions of dollars in investment but also on ensuring Zambian businesses participate in the supply chains created by that investment.
"If a mine is going to spend $2 billion or $3 billion [€1.7 billion to €2.6 billion] to expand that mine, that $3 billion has to go to the people, the people that are small businesses."
Greater local participation, Muyembe argues, could help create businesses and employment while allowing Zambia to retain more of the wealth generated from its natural resources.
The challenge is particularly important for young Zambians, whose expectations extend beyond political stability to jobs and opportunities.
Five years to shape a legacy

Despite his criticism of the political environment surrounding the election, Muyembe told DW that Hichilema still has an opportunity to determine how his second presidency will ultimately be remembered.
He pointed to former Zambian President Levy Mwanawasa, whose disputed 2001 election was followed by a presidency that later gained broader respect.

"I think he has a chance, basically, to redeem himself from the dent of these elections because it also happened with Mwanawasa. I think Mwanawasa's elections were also looked at funny, but he redeemed himself in the way he governed the following year."
That leaves Hichilema with two closely connected tests over the next five years.
One is economic: whether improving headline indicators can translate into jobs, stronger local businesses and better living standards.

The other is democratic: whether opposition voices can operate freely, institutions can command public trust and political competition can take place without eroding Zambia's long-standing tradition of peaceful transfers of power.

The crowds celebrating at Heroes Stadium showed the hope that still surrounds Hichilema among his supporters. The disputed election and its aftermath revealed the mistrust that exists among many other Zambians.
How he governs both groups may ultimately determine not only Hichilema's legacy, but the kind of democracy Zambia carries into its next political chapter.
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: Invasive tropical mosquito found breeding in east London
articles.summary:
Climate crisis could increase incursions of Aedes aegypti, which can transmit Zika virus and dengue, experts say

An invasive mosquito capable of transmitting tropical diseases has been found…

blocks.text: An invasive mosquito capable of transmitting tropical diseases has been found breeding in homes in east London, with experts warning that the rapidly warming climate will lead to greater “incursions of invasive mosquitoes”.
This is the first time the species has been identified breeding in the UK and the fourth time it has been detected.

Aedes aegypti, which are normally found in tropical and subtropical regions, can transmit dengue, chikungunya and Zika virus in countries where these infections are circulating. While none of these diseases are deadly, they can cause complications, with Zika linked to serious problems during and after pregnancy.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the public was low, with no evidence that the mosquitoes in east London have have caused human infections.

The initial finding was reported through UKHSA’s mosquito watch surveillance scheme. The agency said the species could have come into the UK in vehicles, baggage and imported plants and, if the insects found a suitable climate, they could survive.
It said that despite evidence of breeding, the species was not established in the UK and could not survive for long in the typical UK climate, which was too cold.
However, the agency warned that in a warming climate, “we will continue to see incursions of invasive mosquitoes, and increased reports of them being able to survive in the UK”.

David Smith, the advocacy and social change manager at the charity Buglife, said the rapidly warming climate was creating conditions that were more favourable for exotic and potentially invasive species to establish in the UK.

A study earlier this year found that chikungunya, an excruciating tropical disease, can now be transmitted in most of Europe because of higher temperatures caused by the climate crisis. The analysis was the first to assess the effect of temperature on the incubation time of the virus in the Asian tiger mosquito.

Smith said: “Recent reports of non-native invertebrates, including mosquito species, highlight the urgent need for the government to strengthen biosecurity, improve surveillance and address pathways such as the movement of potted plants and soils, through which numerous invertebrates can hitchhike undetected.”
The UKHSA said control measures had been implemented to destroy the larvae, and the area would continue to be monitored closely to identify and eradicate any further mosquitoes and larvae.

It advised residents to remove standing water from gardens and outdoor spaces, including from buckets, containers, paddling pools and plant pots, to reduce opportunities for all species of mosquitoes to breed.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan orders Manuel Bonoan’s release after junking of 5th Division cases
articles.summary: The former Department of Public Works and Highways chief is on bail for the 2nd Division case, while the 5th Division recently dropped the cases against Bonoan following a request from the Office of…

blocks.text: BONOAN. Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan arrives at the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for the arraignment of his graft case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler

The former Department of Public Works and Highways chief is on bail for the 2nd Division case, while the 5th Division recently dropped the cases against Bonoan following a request from the Office of the Ombudsman

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan ordered the release of former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) secretary Manuel Bonoan following the dismissal of his plunder and graft cases before the 5th Division.

“Accordingly, the oral motion of Atty. [Steffanie] Ong is hereby granted. The Commitment Orders (Pending Trial) issued by this court against Manuel Manligas Bonoan in Crim. Case No. E-SB26CRM0005 and Crim. Case No. E-SB26CRM0006, dated June 19, 2026, are hereby recalled,” said a portion of the resolution dated Thursday, September 3.

“Police Brigadier General Portia B. Manalad of the Philippine National Police (PNP) Health Service General Hospital is hereby ordered to release from custody Manuel Manligas Bonoan, unless he is being detained for other lawful reason,” it added.

Bonoan is facing two sets of cases before the Sandiganbayan, where Senator Jinggoy Estrada is also accused: one count of graft at the 2nd Division, and a count of plunder and graft at the 5th Division.

The former DPWH chief is on bail for the 2nd Division case, while the 5th Division recently dropped the cases against Bonoan following a request from the Office of the Ombudsman. This paved the way for Bonoan’s temporary freedom.

The Ombudsman sought the junking of cases against Bonoan because he is the latest prospect to be a state witness in the multibillion flood control scandal. This bid, however, is still uncertain because while he is on bail at the 2nd Division, the said division rejected the motion that sought the dismissal of the graft case.
In June, the Ombudsman announced its intention to put the former DPWH chief on the list of state witnesses.
It believes that Bonoan’s testimony can pin former speaker Martin Romualdez and shed light on how lawmakers allegedly inserted allocations in the national budget through the DPWH. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate asks COA for list of fraudulent, substandard flood control projects
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito said the Senate has asked the Commission on Audit (COA) to provide a list of flood control projects that its ongoing fraud audits have found to be fraudulent or substandard.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 8:49pm
Senator JV Ejercito said the Senate has asked the Commission on Audit (COA) to provide a list of flood control projects that its ongoing fraud audits have found to be fraudulent or substandard.
In an ambush interview on Thursday, Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Finance Committee, said the list would help lawmakers determine which projects should proceed and which should be scrapped.
“We asked them for their cooperation as we resumed the flood control projects," he said.
“We would need a list of projects sa investigation nila that are fraudulent or substandard para at least alam natin kung which projects can be completed, yung pwede ituloy at hindi pwede ituloy."
(We would need a list of projects from their investigation that are fraudulent or substandard so that we know which projects can be completed, which can proceed and which cannot.)

Meanwhile, Ejercito said the Senate has asked concerned agencies to clarify the joint circular governing confidential and intelligence funds and consider issuing clearer guidelines and safeguards following controversies over their use.

On the Senate’s plan to hold budget hearings alongside plenary sessions, Ejercito said the arrangement may begin next week, as agencies still need to be informed and are simultaneously attending House budget hearings.
He described the scheduling as a major challenge given the simultaneous impeachment proceedings, plenary sessions, and budget deliberations.
“Very, it’s really a challenge,” he said.
“Extraordinary talaga itong time na ito because of the impeachment and the plenary and the ongoing budget hearings.”
(This is really an extraordinary time because of the impeachment, plenary sessions, and ongoing budget hearings.)

Ejercito said he had appealed to committee vice chairs to follow, as much as possible, the schedules to be published by the Legislative Budget Research and Monitoring Office (LBRMO) or the Finance Committee.
He acknowledged that senators may have to move quickly between budget hearings and plenary sessions if a vote is suddenly required.

Ejercito also clarified that the arrangement would apply to the Finance Committee given the exceptional circumstances. He said he had raised concerns that the proposed nearly two-week marathon schedule for the impeachment proceedings could significantly affect the budget hearings.
“Dalawa yung choice natin, tapusin yung impeachment or magka-reenacted budget tayo," he said.
(We have two choices: finish the impeachment proceedings or have a reenacted budget.)
He said the Senate is discussing how to fit the budget hearings into the impeachment and plenary session schedules.
“We do not want a reenacted budget as well,” Ejercito said. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Nvidia to buy Hugging Face in $12.93 billion deal
articles.summary: The acquisition of the AI software platform will keep it as an open platform, Nvidia said.

image.caption: The chipmaking giant is seeking to diversify its hold on the AI sector [FILE: Jul 16, 2025]Image: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia will acquire artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion (roughly €11.13 billion), the AI chipmaking giant announced on Thursday.

"Together, we will scale Hugging Face's platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a post on the company's website.
What is Hugging Face and why does its open model stand out?
Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by three French entrepreneurs in New York. The company describes itself as "the AI community building the future."
It touts open models that can be downloaded and modified, in contrast to closed models such as rivals OpenAi or Anthropic.

"Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem. Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want," Huang wrote when announcing the acquisition. "Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face."
Nvidia, best known for its GPUs, specialized chips originally designed to render gaming graphics at high speed, has released over 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets.

articles.title: South Africa airline behind viral stadium flyby scraps repeat display
articles.summary: Two passenger jets passed close to Cape Town's DHL Stadium during a flyover last weekend. The carrier said it has shelved plans to repeat the display as South Africa's aviation authority investigates…

image.caption: About 56,000 people were in Cape Town's DHL stadium when the jets flew overheadImage: Stringer/REUTERS

blocks.text: South African aviation authorities are reviewing a low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger planes at an international rugby match in Cape Town last weekend.

The regional airline, meanwhile, said it had canceled another flypast scheduled for Saturday's rugby test between South Africa and New Zealand in Johannesburg this weekend, citing unfavorable weather.

In a statement, the South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it was carrying out a "compliance verification" of the August 29 flyover at Cape Town's DHL stadium to ensure "all safety protocols were adhered to by the crew."
Footage of the flyby, showing two planes in formation passing over the crowd, was widely shared on social media and prompted discussion about potential safety risks.
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the lead aircraft passed less than 15 meters (50 ​feet) above the top of the packed stadium.
What did SACAA and Airlink say?
The SACAA said it was analyzing flight data provided by Airlink and would go over additional information requested from the carrier before issuing a report.
The regulator said the airline had made applications for the flyovers, which were approved in line with the requirements for special air events.
Airlink, for its part, said the maneuver had been carefully planned and rehearsed, with safety being "the first consideration at every stage of the process."
It said each aircraft had three senior captains on board with a combined 75,000 hours of flying experience.
Nevertheless, it also recognized what it described as the "valid questions and concerns."

Airlink Chief Executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said the decision had been made to withdraw plans for this weekend's stadium flypast in Johannesburg because "the forecast weather points to unfavorable ⁠conditions for a ​safe formation flyby."
A history of flybys in rugby

Stadium flybys have long been tradition at major rugby matches in South Africa, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept overhead before the Springboks faced the All Blacks.
The SACAA said in a statement that South Africa "is ranked seventh globally and first in Africa for our aviation safety standards by the International Civil Aviation Organization."
There have been no fatal accidents in its commercial airline operations space for over four decades, it added.

articles.title: ‘We need a touch of humanity’: Swedish MP promises help for Britons facing deportation if party wins power
articles.summary:
Niels Paarup-Petersen says a law change can end the plight of British citizens caught out by harsh post-Brexit policy as general election looms

A leading Swedish opposition party has…

blocks.text: A leading Swedish opposition party has promised an urgent reprieve for British nationals facing deportation from the country over Brexit administrative issues.

blocks.caption: Joyce Thomas, 78, is facing removal from Sweden due to its hardline Brexit policy. Photograph: Felix Andler

blocks.text: Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, said it would introduce laws to end the suffering of people such as the 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas if, as polls project, it forms a new centre-left coalition after the general election in 10 days’ time. Thomas has been told to leave by next Wednesday after 21 years in Sweden.
Paarup-Petersen said if his party got into power it would reopen the application process so British citizens threatened with deportation could reapply to stay in Sweden.

He said: “We have seen many appalling cases, people who are in a vulnerable state who have every right to be here but are being denied that right because of a minor administrative problem. There has been no leeway whatsoever.
“People are paying the price, but Sweden doesn’t win either. We need a slight touch of humanity here.”

His declaration comes after a British man was detained in Stockholm by police on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation, the latest in a string of cases involving British citizens in the past month.

The man’s wife pleaded with Andy Burnham to intervene, but so far no British politician, or official at the European Commission, has commented on the controversy which the Left party has said was “damaging” relations with the UK at the time of a potential reset with the EU.

blocks.caption: John Sellers with his wife, Caroline. He was deported from Sweden in January despite living there since childhood. Photograph: John Sellers

blocks.text: Al Pinkerton, the Europe spokesperson for the UK’s Liberal Democrat party, also called on Burnham to intervene: “This is the human cost of Brexit: British citizens who built their lives in Europe decades ago now facing detention and deportation.

“The extraordinarily high refusal rate in Sweden should set alarm bells ringing in Downing Street. Andy Burnham must urgently raise these cases with the Swedish government and demand that the protections promised to British citizens under the withdrawal agreement are being honoured.”
Paarup-Petersen’s intervention comes amid growing controversy over what he says is the “appalling” approach of Sweden’s current right-wing government towards British citizens caught out by Brexit.

He said Sweden’s hardline approach to immigration seemed to have infected the approach taken to its obligations under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was a legally binding treaty designed to give lifelong rights to EU citizens in the UK before Brexit and British nationals living in the EU before the end of the transition period in 2021.

“Unfortunately I am not surprised because there is no middle ground here on migration. It is just hard rules and there is little consideration of the way people live in reality,” he said. “I was surprised to hear about the number of British people living here who did not know about the application deadline and that is a big issue.”
Paarup-Petersen said the European Commission should be able to help but “this is a problem that we can solve in Sweden” quickly with the help of the British embassy.

blocks.caption: George Mason, who has dementia and faces deportation, with his daughter Michelle. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family

blocks.text: “We have an election in a week and I hope we can change things quickly because this is very much a Swedish problem as it looks like other countries in the EU do not have the same problem.”

Sweden goes to the polls next Sunday with recent polling showing four centre-left parties including the Centre party and the Social Democrats on track to unseat the government’s centre-right coalition.
Two weeks ago the centre left held a 10 percentage point lead for the 13 September ballot, according to an opinion poll by the public broadcaster SVT.
Paarup-Petersen’s promise comes after weeks of revelations about British citizens who had made Sweden their home long before Brexit who had received removal orders or had already been deported.
They include Thomas, a former nurse who has told how she is “sick” with worry at the prospect of leaving her home and proximity to her son, grandchildren and her husband’s grave.

Others include 34-year-old John Sellers, who was deported in January, even though he has lived in the country since he was 10 years old and George Mason, 74, who needs round-the-clock care for dementia and who has lived in Sweden for 25 years.

Paarup-Petersen said the wider immigration system in Sweden was “messed up”, with one case of a 95-year-old wheelchair-bound Iraqi woman who was told she would be deported after 20 years in the country.

articles.title: Teodoro to colleagues: Pass CADENA transparency bill so we can fight floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Marikina Rep. Marcelino Teodoro has appealed to his colleagues in the House of Representatives to pass a bill that mandates transparency in the budget-making process. He…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Marikina Rep. Marcelino Teodoro has appealed to his colleagues in the House of Representatives to pass a bill that mandates transparency in the budget-making process.
He believes the measure can be a tool to check whether infrastructure projects are implemented properly so that it can deter floods.

In a statement on Wednesday, Teodoro said that the proposed Citizen Access and Disclosure of Expenditures for National Accountability (CADENA) Act Will strengthen accountability in government projects.
He noted that the legislative piece will also allow citizens to scrutinize where public funds are going.
CADENA is a measure marked as a priority bill by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., but it has not been approved on third reading in the House.
The Senate, on the other hand, approved in December 2025 its version of the bill which seeks to put budget documents in a blockchain (shared digital database) accessible to the people.

“Of course, the CADENA Bill is expected to be a priority bill for the second regular session so that the access to information and to procurement will be more transparent and accountability will come true,” Teodoro said.
According to Teodoro, if the measure was already available, it would have allowed people to check on the flood control projects and pressure authorities to perform properly.
He believes it would have avoided the floods that Central Luzon and the National Capital Region (NCR) experienced in recent weeks.

Under the CADENA Act, all government agencies are mandated to upload and regularly maintain detailed budget-related documents — from contracts, project costs, bills of materials and procurement records on a digital platform.
Last December 15, 2025, the Senate passed Senate Bill No. 1506 after 17 senators voted in the affirmative, with no one voting in the negative or abstaining.
This act will enact the establishment of a National Budget Blockchain System, which will record and monitor all stages of the national budget process.
All records of the national budget, including project allocations, disbursements, and procurement transactions, will then be registered in the blockchain as Digital Public Records.
Senator Bam Aquino, the principal author of Senate Bill No. 1506, hailed its passage.

In a statement last November 2025, Aquino said there are stiff penalties that await government officials and agencies that fail to disclose all government transaction documents involving public funds.
“Once the Cadena Act is enacted, the people will be able to see and monitor where every peso funded by the government goes,” Aquino said in a Facebook post on Monday. /apl

articles.title: Solon calls for additional P30B for DOTr’s proposed budget for 2027
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Cagayan de Oro 2nd District Rep. Rufus Rodriguez on Thursday called for the provision of an additional P30 billion to the proposed budget of the Department of Transportation…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Cagayan de Oro 2nd District Rep. Rufus Rodriguez on Thursday called for the provision of an additional P30 billion to the proposed budget of the Department of Transportation (DOTr) for next year to support the agency’s projects, particularly the Mindanao Railway.
During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the DOTr, Rodriguez made a manifestation expressing support for the agency’s funding.

The agency shared that it was given a budget of P300.960 billion under the National Expenditure Program (NEP), which is a 52.52 percent increase from the 2026 NEP of P197.331 billion and 118.33 percent jump from the 2026 General Appropriations Act of P137.846 billion.

“I am therefore constrained in the proper time to move for the approval of the budget of the DOTr plus maraming projects na hindi nafunded. I would like to propose to the plenary that we give additional P30 billion from the P300 billion,” Rodriguez said.

Rodriguez then pointed out that a portion of the proposed additional P30 billion should be allocated for the Mindanao Railway Project. According to the DOTr, the railway project is one of the four foreign-assisted projects that are not allocated budget under the 2027 NEP.
Transport Secretary Giovanni Lopez shared that the agency is already in the final stage of the project’s pre-feasibility study and will soon begin its feasibility study.
“That is why I propose additional P30 billion so that part of that will go to the Mindanao Railway for the local funding and then of course for the feasibility study,” Rodriguez added.

Lopez then welcomed Rodriguez’ support to the agency, particularly to the Mindanao Railway project. He also underscored the importance of distributing transport projects outside Metro Manila to improve and ease mobility of many Filipinos.

“In the P30 billion na ibibigay sana ng Kongreso ay sapat po yan, talagang malaking tulong po sa Kagawaran ng Transportasyon upang sa mga ganitong pagpaplano mas lalo na ‘ho sa Mindanao, sa Visayas, kailangan na po nating lumabas sa Metro Manila ay meron na po tayong magandang feasibility study at pag-aaral po pagdating sa transportation,” the secretary said.

(This P30 billion will be enough and will be a big help for the Department of Transportation so we can also distribute projects in Mindanao and Visayas and we can have a good feasibility study for our transportation.)

Other lawmakers such as Quezon City Rep. and House panel on transportation chairperson Franz Pumaren, Negros Oriental Rep. Isabel Sagarbarria, Ako Bicol Party-list Rep. Jan Franz Chan, and 1-Rider Party-list Rep. Rodge Gutierrez also expressed their support in increasing the funds of the agency.
Despite having a bigger proposed budget in 2027, the DOTr shared that of the 179 projects it proposed for next year, only 30 of these were given funding under the NEP. /mr

articles.title: South Cotabato co-op asks for power conservation amid short supply
articles.summary: KORONADAL CITY — The South Cotabato Electric Cooperative I (SOCOTECO I) urged consumers in South Cotabato to conserve electricity on Thursday, Sept. 3. The request was made as a power supply shortage…

blocks.text: KORONADAL CITY — The South Cotabato Electric Cooperative I (SOCOTECO I) urged consumers in South Cotabato to conserve electricity on Thursday, Sept. 3.
The request was made as a power supply shortage prompted red and yellow alerts across the Mindanao grid and raised the possibility of rotational brownouts.
The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) placed the Mindanao grid under red alert from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m., and yellow alert from 10 a.m. to noon, and again at 10 p.m.

In their official social media page, SOCOTECO I said the alerts were caused by forced outages and reduced capacity at several power plants, leaving available supply insufficient to meet electricity demand.
NGCP also advised that Manual Load Dropping (MLD), which can result in temporary power interruptions in selected areas, may be put in place from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m.
This option is intended to help maintain the stability of the Mindanao grid.
SOCOTECO I was among the electric cooperatives and power distributors identified by NGCP as potentially affected by the measure.
The cooperative said rotational brownouts may be implemented in selected areas, depending on the actual condition of the grid and instructions from NGCP.
It urged its member-consumer-owners to reduce electricity use, particularly during periods of high demand in the afternoon and evening.
NGCP said the planned load dropping can be canceled if grid conditions improve, including a situation wherein the actual electricity demand turns out lower than projected.
Aside from SOCOTECO I, the NGCP advisory covered several other electric cooperatives and distribution utilities across Mindanao.
These cooperatives are SOCOTECO II, SUKELCO, MAGELCO, COTELCO, Davao Light and Power Co. and other utilities in the Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Caraga and Davao regions.
SOCOTECO I said it will issue updates through its official communication channels. /apl

articles.title: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors
articles.summary:
Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes

  • Get our

blocks.text: Memory is an imperfect thing: research shows that recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ to those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence.

“What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney.
“Sometimes they confuse one episode with another,” she said. Paterson’s work has important implications for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence and how their testimony is received.

“If they’re saying this in trial, it’s defence 101 to say … they’ve made this inconsistency, therefore their whole memory is unreliable,” she said. “But we do know what they do report tends to be highly accurate in that it did happen to them. It’s just they might mix up the episode in which it happened.”

Paterson’s work has also found that repeated-event witnesses are perceived to be “less honest, less cognitively competent, and less overall credible than the single-event witnesses – which is pretty concerning that the more repeatedly you are victimised, the less credible you appear to others”.
In recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor testimony in such cases, Paterson was awarded a prestigious Eureka prize on Thursday night.
Established in 1990, the Australian Museum Eureka prizes recognise the work of Australian scientists and science communicators.
Paterson was recognised for excellence in forensic science – one of 19 categories – at an event at Sydney town hall.
She hopes the award will help elevate the voices of victim-survivors. “Often we don’t give them the support and encouragement, and we don’t believe them and see them as credible as we should.”

blocks.caption: Assoc Prof Jane Tiller was recognised at the Eureka prizes for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results. Photograph: Michelle McFarlane/Australian Museum

blocks.text: Also among the winners was Assoc Prof Jane Tiller of Monash University, recognised for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results.

Passed into law in April, the ban will come into effect on 8 October. The legal change will enable scientists to use genomics more effectively to prevent conditions such as cancer and heart disease, Tiller said.
“The biggest reason that people don’t want this testing is because of fear of insurance discrimination,” she said. The legal change was a “critical barrier that we needed to remove”.

“We want to … start finding young people who we know have very high risks of diseases that we can prevent, and give them the screening, the surveillance, the health tools available to them to prevent or treat those diseases early.”

Prof Georgina Long, who alongside the late Prof Richard Scolyer was named Australian of the Year in 2024, won the Eureka prize for scientific research, for her pioneering melanoma work. Four other Australians of the Year have previously received Eureka prizes: Prof Tim Flannery, Prof Ian Frazer, Prof Michelle Simmons, and the late Prof Alan Mackay-Sim.

Also among Thursday night’s winners were Australia’s marine heatwaves forecasting tool, developed by the CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology; the Women’s Microbiome Innovation Group, a Melbourne-based research collaboration that discovered that bacterial vaginosis is sexually transmitted between partners; and Prof Yansong Shen at the University of New South Wales, who developed a scalable low-cost process to recover valuable metals and silicon from used solar panels.

Kim McKay, Australian Museum director and chief executive, said: “This year’s winners are tackling some of our greatest challenges: protecting our environment, advancing healthcare, informing public policy and inspiring the next generation of scientists.
“World-changing discoveries do not happen overnight. They are built on years of dedication, collaboration and sustained investment.”

articles.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
articles.summary: Despite a slew of negative headlines, the German economy has posted its best figures in years. There are reasons for optimism but structural issues remain.

image.caption: There are signs that Germany's economy may have bottomed outImage: Gregor Fischer/Getty Images

blocks.text: The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums.

The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters.

Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026.
Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August.
"It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, President of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery."
"The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro, told DW.

However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said.
Where has the good news come from?
The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up.

Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds.

This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards.

blocks.caption: Low water levels on the Rhine hit economic activity this summerImage: Dominik Bund/IMAGO

blocks.text: Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war.

Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year.

Brzeski says many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefitted from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil.
"There was a bit of a re-channeling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he says.

The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identifies this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks."
It says that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains.

"Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added.
Can the German government take some credit?
Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026.
"It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," says Fuest.
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses

The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness.

It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," says Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy."
Germany's structural problems remain
Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain.

The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined.

"Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" says Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist.

"Chinese competition is still there," he says. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse.
Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses

Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands.

In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums.
For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable.

blocks.caption: Germany's industrial backbone remains intactImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It could hardly have gotten much worse," says Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder 3.0, we have to keep that in mind."

He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve.

"They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he says. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival."

For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He says that three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows.
"It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he says.
