articles.title: Cavite cop’s bro tagged for ‘manipulating’ assault case probe – Napolcom
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A police captain from Cavite, who is the brother of another police officer who supposedly assaulted and threatened to kill a college student, allegedly intimidated and pressured…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A police captain from Cavite, who is the brother of another police officer who supposedly assaulted and threatened to kill a college student, allegedly intimidated and pressured the investigator to manipulate the filing of the case against his brother, the National Police Commission (Napolcom) said.

Napolcom Commissioner Rafael Vicente Calinisan revealed this on Thursday after noting that the cases lodged against the police officer who assaulted the student, Police Senior Master Sergeant Don Carlos Almonidovar from the General Trias Component City Police Station, were “watered down.”

The case investigator only filed grave threats and physical injuries against Almonidovar after the 20-year-old college student, identified only as alias “Ace,” reported the “assault” to the Napolcom on Wednesday.
“Bakit ito yung mga naging kaso niya? Ba’t mababa yung kaso niya, patrolman?” Calinisan asked the investigator, Patrolman Rolyn Pagayon, in a press conference on Thursday.
(Why are these the only cases filed? Why is his case so low, patrolman?)

Responding to this, the patrolman said he was supposed to file an attempted homicide case against Almonidovar since there was really “an intent to kill” when he rammed the motorcycle of the college student.
But he said that as he was conducting an investigation, the suspect’s brother, Police Captain Gerald Nikko Carlos Almonidovar, supposedly called and texted him to manipulate the case.
“May mga sina-suggest, sir, kaya hindi talagang kung ano ang nararapat na kaso ang isinampa ko po,” the investigator said.
(There are suggestions, sir, so what I filed is not really the appropriate case.)
When clarified by Calinisan if the police captain “pressured” him to help his brother’s case, the patrolman replied, “Yes, Sir.”
“Nahirapan kang suwayin kasi ikaw ay patrolman lamang, tama?” the Napolcom commissioner further asked, in which the partrolman also answered in the affirmative.
(It became difficult for you to disobey him because you are only a patrolman, right?)
Calinisan then showed to members of the media the screenshots of the series of text messages between the police captain and the investigator.
Based on the messages, the police captain told the investigator to include in his report that the two students were drunk and exclude that his brother was intoxicated when the incident happened.
The police captain also supposedly ordered that the video showing the incident not be released.
“Di ba klarong obstruction of justice ito?” Calinisan emphasized.
(Isn’t this clearly obstruction of justice?)
The Napolcom commissioner then directed the conduct of a motu proprio investigation against the police captain.

Following the incident, Calinisan said they will study whether cases involving police officers should be assigned to more senior and experienced investigators to prevent supposed intimidation from happening again.
‘File appropriate charges vs. cop who assaulted student’
Meanwhile, Calinisan ordered the Trece Martires City Police Station to file the appropriate charges against the police officer who supposedly assaulted the student.
He also appealed to Land Transportation Office chief Markus Lacanilao to revoke the license of the police officer for driving while intoxicated.
“Sabagay, hindi naman niya kailangan ng lisensya sa loob ng kulungan, pero baka dapat i-revoke din natin yung kaniyang lisensya kasi nag-drive siya under the influence,” he said.
(Actually, he doesn’t need a license inside the prison, but maybe we should revoke his license because he drove under the influence.)

According to the college student, the police officer allegedly rammed his motorcycle, assaulted him, struck him with a firearm, cursed at him, and threatened to kill him after he made a U-turn ahead of the officer’s car along Governor’s Drive in Barangay San Agustin in Trece Martires City at around 11:30 p.m. last Aug. 27.
Following this, the student, along with his 19-year-old companion, was also reportedly brought to the police station to attempt to settle the dispute. /gsg

articles.title: COA eyeing modified rules on confidential funds
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) is studying the possibility of modifying its 11-year-old circular being used as a basis in auditing confidential and intelligence funds, COA…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) is studying the possibility of modifying its 11-year-old circular being used as a basis in auditing confidential and intelligence funds, COA Commissioner Douglas Malillin said on Thursday.

Amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, COA’s Joint Circular (JC) No. 2015-01 with the Department of Budget and Management, the Department of the Interior and Local Government, the Government Commission for GOCCs, and the Department of National Defense has frequently been the subject of debate, particularly in its enactment.

“After all the concerns and issues that were raised regarding the confidential funds, we were taking a look at the joint memorandum circular, which was issued in 2015… and we find that there are certain revisions that need to be modified or revised,” Malillin said.
Malillin enumerated some of the provisions in the circular that they may reform.
These include the supporting documents or documents evidencing payments, particularly the data that should be included, and how auditors will identify sufficiency of the documents.
He also mentioned that there may be a need to have requirements for people who have knowledge of the identities of people using aliases, should they be allowed.
“The present joint memorandum circular does not exactly prohibit nor does it really straightforwardly allow the use of aliases,” Malillin pointed out.

Malillin also mentioned that the current JC lacks provisions on evidence of success and casual links, which he characterized as “very crucial features” on the payment of rewards – an allowable use for confidential funds.

Furthermore, Mallilin noted the need for COA to also identify informants for confidential activities for purposes of auditing.“There should be a balance between protecting the identity, but also a point of where COA, based on certain clearances, can actually take a look at the identity of the person without compromising national security and the confidentiality of the activity,” he explained.
The specific steps in issuing credit notices and notices of disallowance must also be revisited, Mallilin pressed.

A credit notice is issued when an agency passes an audit, while a notice of disallowance is issued to agencies that have been flagged by COA for discrepancies in use or documentation of government funds. /gsg

articles.title: DAR: Decades-long farm lot distribution program may be completed in 2027
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) is on track to distribute remaining farmlots to landless tillers, officials said on Thursday. Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) is on track to distribute remaining farmlots to landless tillers, officials said on Thursday.

Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III told the Inquirer about 20,000 hectares remain from the 5.4 million targeted for distribution under the nearly four-decade-old Comprehensive Agrarian Reform law. The budget department allotted funding for 20,000 hectares of lots for distribution next year, according to DAR Undersecretary Kazel Celeste.

DAR was allotted P4.1 billion for its land tenure security program, funding its land distribution scheme, based on the agency’s 2027 National Expenditure Program. For next year, it was earmarked P14.69 billion.
Celeste warned the amount allotted for land distribution next year may fall short of funding needs, though Estrella offered an optimistic outlook.

“We are not worrying about those things,” he told the Inquirer on the sidelines of the agency’s congressional budget hearing. Estrella said the agency had “many ways” of distributing the land without funding being a constraint.
“It depends on being innovative and creative,” he said, without elaborating.
Land reform is a contentious issue in the Philippines, an agricultural country where vestiges of Spanish colonial land ownership have endured for decades, concentrating possession among a few.
About 47 percent of the country’s total land area is agricultural land, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
Achieving next year’s distribution target may hinge on “cleansing” land records to drop parcels with technical or documentary flaws, according to Tim Salomon of advocacy group Task Force Mapalad.
“One hectare removed from the list is one farmer left landless,” he said.
Salomon said the land distribution program “is severely underfunded,” casting doubt on whether DAR’s budget next year will be enough for the agency to complete its apportionment of farmlots. /mr

articles.title: Senate panel OK’s proposed 2027 Ombudsman’s budget of P7.232B
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.232-billion budget of the Office of the Ombudsman for 2027 has been approved by the Senate Committee on Finance, according to a statement issued by Senior Deputy…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.232-billion budget of the Office of the Ombudsman for 2027 has been approved by the Senate Committee on Finance, according to a statement issued by Senior Deputy Majority Leader JV Ejercito, the committee chair.
The Ombudsman had originally submitted a total budget request of P12.797 billion to the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).

Among its additional funding requests is P168 million for the creation of the Ombudsman Marshal Service, which will include 100 new positions tasked with serving cyber warrants, securing evidence, enforcing orders, and protecting investigators.
According to Ejercito, this is one of the initiatives that the committee intends to support.

“I think the establishment of the Ombudsman Marshal Service will be very important to the performance of their duties. The personnel directly assigned to the Ombudsman are more dedicated and more vetted than those in other enforcement agencies,” Ejercito said in a statement on Thursday.
Flood control case
During the budget hearing, the Ombudsman also provided an update on cases involving alleged irregularities in flood control projects.

So far, 35 cases have already been filed before the courts, both in the Sandiganbayan and regional trial courts, and 166 cases are undergoing preliminary investigation. The Ombudsman is also conducting 107 lifestyle checks.
Ejercito said the investigations must be allowed to take their course and that those found to have committed wrongdoing should be held accountable.
Confidential funds
The Ombudsman also proposed additional confidential funds amounting to P148 million, while the DBM-recommended amount is P51.47 million.

“We cannot promise that the P148 million being requested by the Ombudsman will be fully restored. But we might add a little, especially after hearing what programs and investigations could be affected,” Ejercito said.
He emphasized, however, that confidential funds must remain subject to accountability and existing rules.

“Confidential funds do not mean that they are unaccountable. They still have to be properly justified and used for legitimate investigative purposes. There are instances when they really need to be confidential, particularly in gathering information,” he said.
Ejercito reiterated that the Senate’s policy is to confine confidential funds to law enforcement, national security, and investigative agencies.
Proposed Ombudsman building

Ejercito said the committee would also study the Ombudsman’s proposal for a new building, saying it must first be justified and carefully evaluated, particularly given the government’s limited fiscal space.

He also noted the Ombudsman’s proposal to explore acquiring an existing building instead of constructing a new one, particularly properties that may have been vacated following the closure of some Philippine offshore gaming operator (POGO) facilities.

“If they can find a good deal or bargain for an existing building, that may be more practical than constructing a new one, which could cost much more. But we will have to study the proposal and see if it is justified,” Ejercito said.
He added that any proposed acquisition would still have to go through the appropriate legal and budgetary processes.
The committee’s approval will allow the proposed Ombudsman budget to proceed to plenary deliberations for further scrutiny. /atm

articles.title: DOJ careful in evaluating US extradition bid for Apollo Quiboloy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Department of Justice (DOJ) said it continues to assess the request by the United States to extradite jailed evangelist and alleged sex offender Apollo Quiboloy, as it does not want to take the matter to the court “half-baked.”

Justice Undersecretary Ian Dato said in a news briefing on Thursday that the main factor in determining whether the DOJ should proceed with filing a petition for extradition in a local court is whether the request is “thorough enough” to stand in court.

“The department is conscious of the fact that it should not be filing anything half baked,” Dato stressed. “It will not bound itself to a timeline, but it will make sure that whatever case or petition it will file in court will stand scrutiny by the judge.”

The DOJ received on Aug. 7 the vast amount of documents from the US to boost its request for extradition of Quiboloy, who is facing charges of sex trafficking, visa fraud and cash smuggling in the US.

Chief state counsel Dennis Chan had noted that once the DOJ completes its evaluation and finds that the extradition request was in compliance with the 1994 treaty between the Philippines and the US, a petition would be formally filed before a regional trial court.
However, this could still be challenged by Quiboloy, but only up to the level of the Court of Appeals, based on the Supreme Court’s new extradition rules.
The DOJ also earlier maintained that it is serious in its commitment to international law as well as to a fair judgment of the case. /mr

articles.title: Canadian families still waiting for answers 1 week after Nepal flood disaster
articles.summary: A Toronto woman whose relative is among the missing, said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any…

image.caption: The flooding on Aug. 26 killed at least 1,204 people and left more than 4,200 missing. Nepal's Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while about 590 from 39 countries remain unaccounted for. (Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada·New

A Toronto woman whose relative is among the missing, said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any relatives come up. She's calling for a wider international response to help in rescue efforts as the days tick by with no word on her cousin or the three family members he was travelling with.
29 Canadians among the thousands still missing
Neeral Patel sent well-wishes to her cousin on his birthday last Wednesday, but she never heard back.
Her cousin Ishan Patel was in Nepal at the time, not far from the border with China, where a devastating flash flood ripped through the valley that same day.
She's calling for a wider international response to help in rescue efforts as the days tick by with no word on her cousin or the three family members he was travelling with.
"We want to give a lot of hope. But with each passing day, it's just getting chipped away, and time is of the essence," said Patel, who lives in Toronto.
Ishan Patel was travelling with his wife, Akanksha Patel, both dual Canadian-U. S. citizens, along with his mother, Shilpa Patel, and father-in-law, Umesh Patel, who are Canadian, she said.
The four were on a long-planned pilgrimage to Mount Kaliash ahead of Ishan Patel starting a new job as an orthopedic surgeon, after finishing his fellowship in July, she said.
"It was kind of the big holy beginnings to his new career."
The flooding on Aug. 26 killed at least 1,204 people and left more than 4,200 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while about 590 from 39 countries remain unaccounted for.
Canadian found safe
Ottawa had said 30 Canadians and permanent residents were among the missing. Later Wednesday, it reported that one Canadian citizen was safe, and the tally was changed to 29.
"The individual was unreachable due to communication outages and established contact yesterday," Anita Anand, Canada's foreign affairs minister, said in a statement.
In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.
Why the Nepal flash flood was almost impossible to predict | About That
The scale of the disaster is hampering rescue efforts, as landslides and destroyed roads have cut off remote areas.
Rescuers were also racing to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels.

With so many still unaccounted for, Patel said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any relatives come up.
She said two family members have also travelled to Kathmandu to look in hospitals and anywhere else they can find answers, but the roads up to the flood-hit area are closed.
Making the wait even harder is that they know where to search, she said, because her cousin's phone pinged from a spot a short distance from Hotel Kailash, where they had breakfast last Wednesday.
"This is why we're urging everyone to please, in the right area, search as much as you can, because we're coming up to a week's time and still no news," she said.

Anand said search teams in China and Nepal are using a range of specialized tools and technologies including drones, helicopters, search dogs and other advanced equipment as the ground search continues.

She added that Canada would send more than 18,000 emergency items from Canadian Red Cross stockpiles, including blankets and buckets, to the area in addition to the $5 million Ottawa has already pledged in humanitarian aid.

items: Canadian missing after Nepal flooding found safe, Anand says
Waterloo region, Guelph residents worry for loved ones missing after flash floods in Nepal

blocks.text: "We have a 10-person team on the ground in Nepal. I am in continuous touch with my colleague, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, and we will leave no stone unturned to help Canadians in need."
Patel said Global Affairs told her family about the team being sent but they're still holding out hope for a bigger response.
"There should be a global effort, everyone work together to try to bring our family members home."

articles.title: DFA seeks P35.17-B budget for 2027
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) has proposed a P35.173-billion budget for 2027 to sustain its operations in national security, diplomacy and consular assistance.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 6:24pm
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) has proposed a P35.173-billion budget for 2027 to sustain its operations in national security, diplomacy and consular assistance.

“[The proposed 2027 budget] will enable us to sustain our core operations and respond to the Philippines’ growing requirements in national security, economic diplomacy, consular services, and assistance to national and organizational development,” Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said during the House budget hearing on Thursday.
The proposed 2027 DFA budget is slightly higher than the P34.9-billion allocation for 2026.

Of the proposed budget, P166.940 million is allocated for the Foreign Service Institute, P52.032 million for the UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines, and P51.384 million for the Presidential Commission on Visiting Forces.
The proposed allocation is broken down as follows:

items: Personnel Services (PS): P13.55 billion, or 39%
Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE): P18.836 billion, or 54%
Capital Outlay (CO): P2.515 billion, or 7%

blocks.text: In 2027, the DFA will implement the fourth tranche of salary increases and Foreign Service allowances. It will also transfer the Technical Cooperation Council of the Philippines under the PS budget.

Under the MOOE, the DFA will allocate P2.8 billion for the Next Generation Passport, set aside funds for foreign exchange fluctuations and inflation, and provide additional funding for foreign service personnel and its Information Systems Strategic Plan (ISSP) project.
Under the CO, however, no funds are allocated for car fleet replacement, ISSP projects or new appropriations for the opening of foreign service posts in 2027.
DFA data showed that there are 10.5 million overseas Filipinos worldwide, including 2.7 million overseas Filipino workers. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
articles.summary: Her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem, who became a face of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died, aged 92, her foundation says.
In a post on Instagram, it said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City, "surrounded by many who loved her".
Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance, a group dedicated to fighting sexism, more than 50 years ago.

She started her career as a journalist in New York in the 1970s and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on other women's issues than the perils of housekeeping and the mandates of the beauty industry.
During the 1970s, Steinem was one of the main voices campaigning for women's reproductive rights.

She celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
articles.summary: The trailblazing feminist was an iconic leader of women's rights in the US.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Gloria Steinem pictured in 1990 in her New York City apartment
Gloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement, and her career spanned a myriad of roles that changed the lives of generations of women.

With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.
She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.
Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.
The early years
Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.
Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.
Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations.
As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic Convention

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic Convention
She would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.

In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.

Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.
Breakthrough article

Her big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.
As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitation

blocks.text: Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitation
Using the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.
Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.
Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors.
Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles.

"To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."
All-female journalism
Undaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.
Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s.

"I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.
So she took matters into her own hands.

In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publication

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publication
Critics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".
The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.
In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate.
Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.

By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.
Abortion rights campaigner
Though still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.

At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.

Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."
Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.
She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.

Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane Fonda

blocks.text: Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane Fonda
Steinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".

After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.

The same year she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."
Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum, and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.
Too glamorous?

Critics, however, came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.

Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.
The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activists

blocks.text: Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activists

US President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".
Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.
He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.

As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.

But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down.
"If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.
'I can't mate in captivity'

Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.
They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968).
"I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.
But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.
At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.

But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.
Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.

blocks.caption: Image caption, David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine Rothschild

blocks.text: David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine Rothschild
Bale died three years later from brain lymphoma.
Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.
'So much to do'
Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".
In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.

She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".
In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms Magazine was still publishing.
Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."
She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.
And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

articles.title: Some senators want to revisit 16-vote threshold in Sara Duterte impeachment trial -Zubiri
articles.summary: Some senator-judges want to revisit the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri said Thursday.

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 6:22pm
Some senator-judges want to revisit the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri said Thursday.
In a press conference, the Senate Majority Leader said that some of his colleagues have questioned the threshold, given that some senator-judges could not attend the ongoing trial.

“There were some colleagues who would like to revisit the threshold. Because at that time, wala pa ‘yung mga nawawalang senador. Ngayon kasi, may mga nasa kulungan at isa at-large, pugante-at-large,” he said.
(Some colleagues would like to revisit the threshold. Because at that time when the ruling was made, there were no missing senators. Now, some are in jail, and one is a fugitive at-large.)
When the impeachment trial began on July 6, presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero ruled that 16 affirmative votes of senator-judges are required to convict Duterte in her trial.
Citing the Constitution, Escudero said that no person shall be convicted in an impeachment trial without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.
And with the Senate composed of 24 members, Escudero said a literal interpretation of the constitutional provision means conviction requires at least 16 affirmative votes.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.
Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, has not been attending the trial for weeks now due to health concerns.
Zubiri explained that the best way to address concerns about the voting threshold is “to debate about it and seek a ruling from the presiding officer.”
“It may come up sooner or later. That, I can divulge. There are some questions with some senators on the threshold. So that issue has to be answered soon enough by the presiding officer,” he added.

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol previously said that the 16-vote threshold for convicting the Vice President is already “set in stone” unless the matter is raised before the Supreme Court. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court
articles.summary:
After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’

A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and…

blocks.text: A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention.
The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year.
It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles.
They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children.
In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities.

In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling.
Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling.
On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility.

“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a ‌gradual reunification process, ‌allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend ‌overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said.
In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”.

They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds.
The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”.
“We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote.

“How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents?
“How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?”

Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping.
But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education.
After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen.
The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote.
“We are deeply saddened by this.

“We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.”
The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.

articles.title: More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
articles.summary: Rescuers found 44 survivors on board the vessel but bad weather meant they had to leave five bodies behind.

blocks.text: More than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died in a boat which was adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for 27 days.

Spanish Maritime Rescue teams located the vessel some 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria's coastal town of Arguineguín on Wednesday and found 44 survivors, with five dead bodies also on board.

The boat is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August with 127 occupants on board. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of Spanish charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people had lost their lives.
Rescuers were forced to leave the five bodies they found due to the rough sea conditions, Maritime Rescue said.
The organisation said it could not verify how many people were originally on board the vessel as it was not within its remit.
The 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.
"Once the rescue was complete, adverse weather conditions in the area - featuring 20-knot winds and 2.5m waves - made it impossible to recover the five bodies found on board the vessel," it added.
Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition.
The rest were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, where they disembarked in the early hours of Thursday morning.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92
articles.summary:
Famous for the 1963 exposé in which she worked as a Playboy Bunny, her books and journalism took on many varieties of discrimination

Gloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist…

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist whose activism helped push through greater rights for women around the world has died, aged 92.
Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her”, a statement shared to her Instagram page said.

“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post added. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.”

Steinem brought a feminist perspective into the mainstream through rigorous journalism, public speaking and activism. The author of nine books, she campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, the pornography industry and the Vietnam and Gulf wars. She also worked in support of causes including Black Lives Matter, the reunification of Korea, female reproductive rights, LGBTQ rights and the Times Up movement. In 1984, she was arrested while protesting against apartheid outside the South African embassy in Washington DC.

Born in Ohio in 1934, Steinem grew up in a trailer home. Her mother’s mental illness left her struggling to hold on to work and in and out of sanatoriums. When she was 10, her parents separated and, while growing up in a rundown home in Toledo with her mother, Steinem began to notice the hostility her mother endured as a working woman.

After graduating from a women’s liberal arts college in 1956, Steinem travelled to India for two years, where she worked as a legal clerk in the country’s supreme court. Returning to the US, she worked as the director of the Independent Research Service, a CIA front that recruited American students to disrupt the Soviet-controlled World Youth Festivals in Vienna and Helsinki. Steinem later revealed she had always known who was bankrolling the operation: “If I had a choice I would do it again.”

In 1962, she received her first “serious assignment” in journalism from Esquire magazine editor Clay Felker. Her feature on contraception, The Moral Disarmament of Betty Coed, detailed how women were forced to choose between careers and family. The following year, Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for 11 days, to write her infamous, two-part exposé of how the glamour models were treated while working in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy Club. Forced into tight costumes and high heels, Steinem lost 10lbs – half of them in a single night – during her stint; her manager celebrated by making her costume two inches tighter. Following the article, she was unable to get work because “because I had now become a Bunny – and it didn’t matter why”.

blocks.caption: Steinem in 1977. Photograph: Everett/REX/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In 1968, Felker hired her to work at New York magazine, in which she would coin the term “reproductive freedom” for an article about an abortion “speakout” in Greenwich Village. Having had an abortion in London when was 22, she later described feeling a “big click” while at the protest and said the day marked the start of her life as an “active feminist”.

“I think the person who said: ‘Honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament’ was right,” she told the Observer in 2011. “Speaking for myself, I knew it was the first time I had taken responsibility for my own life. I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life, and therefore it felt positive.”

She also credited black feminists including Florynce Kennedy, Evelyn Cunningham, Shirley Chisholm and Fannie Lou Hamer for teaching her the importance of activism. “It was like finding a family,” she said of that time. “As wildly different as we may be, and we certainly were, women share hopes and a certain vision of the world, and a certain shit detector.”

This also began Steinem’s career as a provocative journalist, penning articles including If Men Could Menstruate, which ran in Ms, a magazine co-founded by Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 1971. The first issue featured Wonder Woman on the cover; the superhero had recently given up her powers to stay with her male love interest, and the essay argued that DC Comics should restore her powers and return the character to her feminist roots. Steinem also wrote articles such as What It Would Be Like If Women Win in Time, and After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, the 1969 New York magazine article that would make her name as a feminist leader.

blocks.caption: Gloria Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 2014. Photograph: Dan Bagan/Museum of the City of New York

blocks.text: Terrified of public speaking and conflict, but media savvy, Steinem used the platform she gained as a white, educated woman to speak out for those traditionally ignored – black people, ethnic minorities and the working class. Sex and race were always intertwined, she argued in 1971, “because they are easy, and visible differences have been the primary ways of organising human beings into superior and inferior groups and into the cheap labour on which this system still depends.” In 2017, she said: “It doesn’t surprise me that the most virulent anti-abortion measures are coming from Alabama and other southern states because racism and sexism are always intertwined. You can’t perpetuate racism without controlling women and reproduction.”

Steinem was also a polarising figure. Some feminists felt her position as a public leader in the movement had been decided not by merit but by the media, which chose her for being young, white and attractive; in her 2015 book My Life on the Road, she wrote that the “idea that whatever I had accomplished was all about looks would remain a biased and hurtful accusation even into my old age”.

She was roundly criticised for decades for a 1998 opinion piece for the New York Times, in which she supported president Bill Clinton in the face of sexual harassment allegations. “He is not guilty of sexual harassment,” she wrote, only “a gross, dumb, and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life”. In 2017, she said: “We have to believe women. I wouldn’t write the same thing now because there’s probably more known about other women now.” She was also regarded as hostile to transgender rights because of a piece she wrote in 1977, a position she clarified in 2013: “I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned.”

In 1986, Steinem was diagnosed with breast cancer, then in 1994 the chronic pain condition trigeminal neuralgia. After years of dismissing marriage, she married environmental activist David Bale in 2000, and remained close with her stepson, the actor Christian Bale, after his father’s death in 2003.

Having supported Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, Steinem was a prominent critic of Donald Trump, co-chairing and speaking at the Women’s March on Washington, a mass protest held the day after the Trump’s inauguration in January 2017. “The only good news of Trump is that the galvanising of activism is like nothing I have ever seen in my life,” she told the Guardian that year. “A thousand times more even than the Vietnam war, and how important that was – or of any other thing I’ve ever seen.”
In 2011, she told the Observer: “I hope to live to 100. There is so much to do.”

articles.title: Victims sue South African government over 1961 Sharpeville massacre that left 91 dead
articles.summary:
Claim relating to infamous apartheid-era shooting of protesters part of wave of litigation for apartheid-era crimes

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South…

blocks.text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress. “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

blocks.caption: Abraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back while protesting against South Africa’s apartheid pass laws during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.  Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.
The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.
Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South Africa government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

blocks.caption: Dead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station. Photograph: PN2

blocks.text: In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission. That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.
Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed that protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Colonel J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

blocks.caption: Members of a choir perform during the commemorations of the massacre, at the Phelindaba cemetery in Sharpeville, on 21 March 2026.  Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.
Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of around 20,000 rand for six years.
“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

blocks.caption: Paulina Mathinye, whose father Samson was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacre Photograph: Rachel Savage/The Guardian

blocks.text: The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father Samson was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.
Mathinye didn’t initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but couldn’t afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems didn’t begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

articles.title: Judge blocks new Trump bid against birthright citizenship – US politics live
articles.summary:
Maryland judge issues preliminary injunction blocking Trump’s executive order targeting what he termed ‘birth tourism’

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

A US…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1m agoApple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
23m agoJudge blocks new Trump bid against birthright citizenship

blocks.text: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.

The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.
Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.

Trump welcomed the news, declaring in a Truth Social post that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.

The US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
Judge blocks new Trump bid against birthright citizenship
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A US federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting who qualifies for birthright citizenship.
The move thwarts President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict the constitutional right, which comes after the US supreme court rejected his previous effort, AFP reported.

US district judge Deborah Boardman of Maryland issued a preliminary injunction following an appeal by rights groups who challenged Trump’s executive order from 6 August targeting what he termed “birth tourism”.

“The supreme court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ’citizens at birth’,” Boardman wrote in her 35-page ruling, adding the president’s August order “is almost certainly unconstitutional”.

“When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the supreme court, and lost again today,” said Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, a Maryland-based group.
Trump’s fresh executive order was aimed at those who he alleges enter the country under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth.

The president’s efforts to curb birthright citizenship are part of his wider campaign to limit immigration, which includes expelling millions of undocumented migrants and removing deportation protections from nationals of more than a dozen countries.
In other developments:

items: House Democrats rejected a constitutional amendment proposed by Republicans to ensure the size of the supreme court is permanently capped at nine justices. The proposal, a Republican effort to make the supreme court a campaign issue ahead of the November midterms, failed 212-206.

House Democratic lawmakers introduced a war powers resolution seeking to stop the Trump administration’s boat strikes. Gregory W Meeks, Adam Smith, Jim Himes and Bennie G Thompson said people have been killed “without due process” in attacks never authorized by Congress.

Senator Richard Blumenthal pushed back against a statement from the US Postal Service about its new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections. “‘Just trust us’ is not acceptable,” he said.

Donald Trump celebrated the news that Apple had fulfilled his request to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for Maps app users in the US following an executive order that came amid rising trade tensions between the US and Canada.
The Pentagon introduced guidelines for the mandatory new ⁠testosterone deficiency screening required for service members age 30 and older, a policy introduced by Pete Hegseth last month.

Trump – claiming that the US has control over the strait of Hormuz despite escalating conflict with Iran and extensive evidence to the contrary – has floated the idea of naming the critical waterway “TRUMP STRAIT”.

articles.title: Watch: US man struck by lightning describes 'horrific' experience
articles.summary: Thomas Fahmy says he saw "a bright white flash" and instantly fell to the ground.

blocks.text: A man struck by lightning as he was walking down the street in Staten Island, United States, has described the experience as "horrific".
Thomas Fahmy said he had been walking to the dentist on 27 August when he saw "a bright white flash" and instantly fell to the ground.
"I've never felt these sensations ever in my life", he told CBS News, BBC News's US partner.
Fahmy was sent to hospital with the help of a local resident who called 911, and did not sustain serious injuries.

articles.title: El Niño takes toll on Bukidnon rice farms
articles.summary: VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — Hundreds of hectares of rice fields in this major agricultural hub have been affected by below-normal rainfall, prompting the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) to…

blocks.text: VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — Hundreds of hectares of rice fields in this major agricultural hub have been affected by below-normal rainfall, prompting the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) to implement scheduled water deliveries.

Valencia City spans a total physical agricultural area of over 10,000 hectares, consisting of 9,862 hectares of irrigated land, 990 hectares of rainfed farms, and 19 hectares of upland fields dedicated to local consumption located in Pantaron, Barangay Banlag.

Adonis Torres, monitoring personnel of the City Agriculture Office, told the Inquirer on Thursday, September 3, that the dry spell has severely impacted both rainfed and downstream agricultural areas.

In Sitio Bantal, Barangay Banlag—which covers over 300 hectares of rainfed rice fields—about 80 percent of the crops have struggled to transition from the vegetative to the reproductive stage due to a severe lack of water.
Torres noted that farmers have exhausted all options, including water pumps, as local water sources have dried up.
While NIA has installed solar-powered pumps in areas like Barangay Laligan, Lumbayao, Lumbo, and upper Kabolooan and Boyog in Barangay Banlag, officials said the supply remains insufficient.
In Lumbayao and Lumbio, solar pumps are still being monitored as farms heavily rely on rainfall.

Meanwhile, areas near rivers like Banlag still have some water supply and remain in the vegetative stage at 70 to 80 percent, but officials warn these crops are not guaranteed to survive if the rivers dry up amid continuous below-normal rainfall.
Conversely, areas with sufficient NIA irrigation, particularly in Laligan, have largely completed harvesting with minimal worries, while downstream areas bear the brunt of the shortage.

For corn crops, Torres reported that while most have already been harvested, ears were notably smaller due to extreme heat and below-normal rains experienced as early as mid-April, affecting around 50 to 100 hectares.
Additionally, about thee hectares of four-month ginger gardens have been affected by the dry conditions.

The agricultural strain comes in the wake of an advisory issued by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) on September 1, warning of unusually high temperatures and a moderate-to-strong El Niño across Mindanao.

Climate models indicate the phenomenon could strengthen toward late 2026 and persist into the first half of 2027, prompting local authorities to initiate water conservation and drought-mitigation measures.
The City Government of Valencia and relevant local departments are continuing monitoring efforts to assist affected farmers as dry conditions persist. /mr

articles.title: NU-MOA: Bomb threat in Pasay campus was a ‘hoax’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National University–Mall of Asia (NU-MOA) in Pasay City said authorities have determined that the alleged bomb threat in its campus early Thursday was a hoax. According to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National University–Mall of Asia (NU-MOA) in Pasay City said authorities have determined that the alleged bomb threat in its campus early Thursday was a hoax.
According to the NU-MOA, its premises have been “cleared and deemed safe,” and no explosive or hazardous materials were found after an inspection by the Pasay City authorities.

Personnel from the PNP MOA Substation K9 unit, Pasay Investigation Division, and the Pasay Bureau of Fire Protection swept the area following the security threat at around 7:50 a.m., the university said.
Meanwhile, afternoon classes resumed. Its morning classes were temporarily held through remote learning modes due to the incident.

“While afternoon classes are expected to resume, we assure our students, faculty, employees, parents and the entire NU community that your safety and security remain our highest priority,” the NU-MOA said earlier.
The NU-MOA urged the public to refrain from spreading unverified information regarding the incident.
It added that announcements or advisories will be posted in its official pages.
“A cyber investigation is underway in coordination with the appropriate offices to trace and verify the source of the threat,” it added. /apl

articles.title: Tarlac lawmaker says she sought funds for collapsed bridges
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tarlac Rep. Maria Cristina Angeles said Thursday that she had long sought government funding to strengthen two bridges that recently collapsed due to heavy rains and strong…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tarlac Rep. Maria Cristina Angeles said Thursday that she had long sought government funding to strengthen two bridges that recently collapsed due to heavy rains and strong river currents.
Angeles said she had asked the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) to address concerns over the foundations of the two bridges even when she was still a mayor.
She was referring to the 136-meter-long Agana Bridge, which collapsed over the weekend, and the 720-meter-long Aquino Bridge, which collapsed on Aug. 28.

“Through the years that I was mayor, I had long asked the DPWH to give sufficient attention to finding a solution to strengthen the foundations of these two bridges, but this was not prioritized by previous officials,” Angeles said in Filipino.
“As a newly seated congresswoman, I personally appealed to Secretary Vince Dizon during the recent budget hearing to provide sufficient funding for the bridges,” she added.
Angeles also thanked President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon for visiting the area to inspect the damage.
“I am deeply grateful to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Secretary Vince for their personal visit, concern, solutions and immediate response,” she said in Filipino.
Angeles also appealed for unity among Tarlac residents and urged them to refrain from politicizing the issue or pointing fingers.
“Instead, let us unite and help one another, and respect the DPWH as it provides the correct information about what happened,” she said in Filipino.
On Wednesday, Marcos and Dizon inspected the ongoing construction of a Bailey bridge intended to restore access following the collapse of Agana Bridge.
The President directed the DPWH to fast-track the construction of the alternate bridge and said the national government would provide P300 million in assistance to the Tarlac City government.
Angeles joined Tarlac City Mayor Susan Yap, Tarlac Gov. Christian Yap and other local officials during the inspection.
Marcos also said Wednesday that widespread flooding in Central Luzon and Metro Manila resulted from the failure to implement a flood control master plan that had existed for decades.
“We already have a master plan; it’s just never been executed,” Marcos said when asked whether the public could expect such a plan.
“We’re only executing it now. We have had a master plan for decades, but nothing was done. Only now. We’re only starting it now,” he added, without specifying which master plan he was referring to.
The remarks came as 9.4 million people, or 2.7 million families, across Luzon were displaced by flooding caused by three storms and the prevailing southwest monsoon, or habagat, since Aug. 1.
On Aug. 29, a sport utility vehicle fell into the Tarlac River as Agana Bridge collapsed. Only one of its five passengers survived.
The remains of two passengers were recovered in Pangasinan, while two others remained missing.
Tarlac was placed under a state of calamity on Aug. 30 following widespread damage caused by the southwest monsoon.

articles.title: The US and Venezuela: a century-old relationship drenched in oil
articles.summary: A visual look at how Washington’s relationship with Caracas has gone from cordial to ‘predatory’
articles.byline: Oliver Holmes, Seán Clarke and Lucy Swan

blocks.text: Written in the middle of the last century, the US Department of State memo conveys its message in a curt and undiplomatically honest tone: the glue that binds Washington to Caracas is, and is always likely to be, oil.
“All US policies toward Venezuela are affected in greater or less degree by the objective of assuring an adequate supply of petroleum for the US,” the 1950 document reads.

Decades later, little appears to have changed. After a brazen night-time kidnapping of the country’s leader earlier this year, Donald Trump announced last week that the US was taking majority control over about a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. That deal, according to the White House, “secures our energy dominance for the next century”. How much it will benefit Venezuelans is yet to be seen.

The country’s importance to the US has been proven time and time again over the past century. Home to what are now known to be the world’s largest known oil reserves, Venezuela kept allied planes, ship and tanks well fuelled during the second world war.

Washington and Caracas largely cooperated over the following decades, with US energy companies heavily involved in Venezuela’s oil industry, and profiting from it immensely. But relations took a nosedive in 1999, when Hugo Chávez became president.

A self-professed socialist and anti-imperialist, Chávez made alliances, and often oil deals, with China, Iran and Russia. Venezuela switched 180 degrees to become a natural adversary of the US, alongside its ally Cuba.

blocks.caption: Hugo Chávez pictured in 2010. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Relations deteriorated further when Chávez was briefly detained by his own military after a deadly crackdown on mass anti-government protests. The attempted overthrow lasted only two days and he was soon back in the presidential palace, accusing Washington of involvement in the failed coup.

Chávez deepened Venezuela’s dependence on oil exports in the years that followed. In 2007, he stepped up his battle with Washington with a wave of nationalisation in which he seized oilfields, including those that US firms had operated.

Caracas had nationalised the oil industry decades before, but had allowed US companies to profit from the extraction. Under Chávez’s new terms, however, the state oil company was given control of a majority share and foreign firms were offered minority stakes.
Among US oil companies, Chevron agreed to the worse terms, but ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips refused and were in effect pushed out of the industry.

Only Chevron, the second largest US oil company, has continued to operate in the country. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips engaged in a years-long legal battle with Venezuela for compensation. The World Bank’s international centre for the settlement of investment disputes awarded them billions of dollars, but Venezuela has never paid the money in full.

Still, much of the country’s oil infrastructure was built with foreign involvement, and foreign companies are still active in the exploitation of the fields, among them Russian, Chinese and Cuban firms, as well as UK and European companies, including Shell, BP, Italy’s Eni and Spain’s Repsol.
When Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro rose to power. The former bus driver had worked as his foreign minister and continued an antagonistic policy towards the US.

Maduro’s rule was considered dictatorial. The UN estimated in 2019 that more than 20,000 Venezuelans had died in extrajudicial killings. Key institutions, such as the judiciary, were eroded under Maduro and the rule of law deteriorated.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Venezuela’s government protesting in Caracas on 3 January 2026 after the US seized Nicolás Maduro.

blocks.text: The US has portrayed the Maduro government as illegitimate. A Washington-led sanctions campaign compounded widespread corruption, and the Venezuelan economy suffered.
It did not help the relationship that Maduro kept close ties with Moscow and Beijing. About 80% of the crude oil Venezuela produced was exported to China before the US-imposed blockade in December.
China is the world’s biggest oil importer, and takes the shipments as repayment for loans it previously gave to Caracas, often at low prices.

Since the start of his second term, Donald Trump had repeatedly called for Maduro to be ousted, accusing him of sending drugs and criminals to the US – a claim experts say lacks evidence. He also claimed Maduro was stealing US oil, a reference to Chávez’s seizure.
In July last year, Washington announced a $50m (£37m) bounty on Maduro’s head, accusing him of being one of the biggest drug traffickers in the world.

Trump’s administration began to carry out airstrikes against alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and then to seize Venezuelan tankers, while building up the US military presence in the waters surrounding the country.

Trump gave Maduro an ultimatum to relinquish power in late November, offering him safe passage out of the country. But Maduro refused the offer, telling supporters he did not want “a slave’s peace” and accusing the US of wanting control of his country’s oil reserves.
This January, in the ultimate expression of a relationship breakdown, US forces carried out a pre-dawn raid on Caracas, capturing Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are now on trial in New York.
Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, initially denounced Maduro’s capture as a kidnapping, but has since shown she is willing to work with Washington.

In the aftermath of Maduro’s abduction, Trump said the US would take control of Venezuela’s oil industry. And in August, after months of secret talks, Washington’s longstanding oil-focused policy was on display again when the US president announced the agreement to control millions of barrels of oil.

A White House press release described the agreement as the “biggest oil deal in world history” that gave the US government “powerful governance rights” over reserves. Further down in the document, the White House claimed private-sector growth would help drive a democratic transition in Venezuela, though few in Caracas will be holding their breath. Rodríguez has already been forced to defend herself against claims she is surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power.

One prominent Venezuelan economist has called the deal “predatory”, saying it was “done at gunpoint”. Francisco Rodríguez wrote that Washington’s actions in Venezuela had turned the country into “a protectorate in all but name”.
“Trying to run a country from the capital of an imperial power has been tried before,” he said. “And it has not ended well.”
​Additional reporting by Jillian Ambrose

articles.title: Why Quebec’s election has been turned upside down
articles.summary: Quebec’s election looked like a foregone conclusion. Then, the trade war hit, and turned the race on its head.

image.caption: The Quebec provincial flag flies on a flag pole in Ottawa, Friday, July 24, 2026 in Ottawa. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Front Burner
Quebec’s election looked like a foregone conclusion. Then, the trade war hit, and turned the race on its head.
LISTEN | FRONT BURNER:
Front Burner26:00Why Quebec’s election has been turned upside down

In just over a month, Quebecers will head to the ballot box. And, until recently, this election seemed like a foregone conclusion: the Parti Quebecois, running on a promise to hold another independence referendum, had been ahead in the polls for the better part of three years.

Then, the Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed, and Quebec’s political future suddenly looks uncertain. The governing Coalition Avenir Quebec has surged from a distant fourth place, the PQ has shelved its referendum until after Donald Trump leaves office, and the U.S. commerce secretary has accused Mark Carney of “manufacturing” a fight over the French language to stop the sovereigntists from winning.
Paul Journet is a political columnist for La Presse, and he unpacks what this election means for the province – and for the rest of the country.
