articles.title: UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
articles.summary: The WMO has warned that the natural weather phenomenon could bring disruption to global economies.
articles.byline: Esme Stallard, Mark Poynting and Becky Dale, Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita Yadav

blocks.text: Image source, Florian Plaucheur/AFP via Getty Images
El Niño brought intense flooding and landslides to southern Brazil in 2024
ByEsme Stallardsenior climate and science reporterMark Poynting and Becky DaleBBC Verify and Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita Yadav
The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.
El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.
Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.

The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.
The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."
El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.
Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.
In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.
But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.
This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.

blocks.caption: A line graph with the caption "El Nino is forecast to be very strong" and sub-headline "Sea surface temperature and forecast temperature in the tropical Pacific compared with 1991-2020 monthly average. A curved line from January 2026 rising to show +2C by July 2026, and then a forecast line from…

blocks.text: Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.
Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.
With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.
It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change.
El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC.
This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover.
"[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed," said Hobday.
Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions.

Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring.
But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried.

blocks.caption: Two maps showing sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean. The map from December 2025 shows cooler-than-usual conditions, marked in blue, indicating a La Niña. The map from July 2026 shows much warmer-than-usual conditions, marked in red, indicating an El Niño.

blocks.text: Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruption
While the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months.
Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires.
On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall.
About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year.

Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year.
A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month".
"The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy.

Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño event

blocks.text: Image source, Monirul Bhuiyan/AFP via Getty Images
Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño event
Stronger typhoons and landslide risk
Thousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño.
In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead.
And in August, more than 1m people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds.
Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding.

blocks.caption: Map of typical effects of El Niño episodes on precipitation patterns for each region. Key trends are drying in many equatorial regions (northern South America, central Africa, South East Asia and Australia), marked in brown. Southern United States generally becomes wetter than normal, marked in g…

blocks.text: "We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO.

This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain.
Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific.

Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away.

Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm."

He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts.

At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak.

However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.

articles.title: DMW told to protect PH seafarers after deadly Strait of Hormuz attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Several senators on Thursday urged the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) to ensure the safety and protection of Filipino seafarers in high-risk areas following the death of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Several senators on Thursday urged the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) to ensure the safety and protection of Filipino seafarers in high-risk areas following the death of two Filipino crew members in an attack on a Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Sen. Raffy Tulfo both called for stronger safety measures for Filipino seafarers and assistance for those affected by the incident.

Their statements came after the DMW confirmed that two Filipino seafarers were killed after the Saudi-flagged M/V SIDR was hit by unknown projectiles while about to traverse the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 31.
Fourteen other Filipino crew members aboard the vessel survived the incident unharmed.

“The deaths of two Filipino seafarers following an attack on a Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker while transiting the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week are deeply unfortunate. The DMW should ensure that the families of the victims, including those who survived the attack, immediately receive all the necessary assistance during this difficult time,” Gatchalian said in a statement.

“Hindi pa tapos ang kaguluhan sa Middle East kaya kailangang siguraduhin ng gobyerno ang kaligtasan ng lahat ng OFWs sa rehiyon, kabilang ang mga Pilipinong marino. Prayoridad dapat ang mahigpit na pagpapatupad ng safety protocols sa mga lugar at bansang itinuturing na high-risk areas,” the Senate president added.

(The conflict in the Middle East is not yet over, so the government must ensure the safety of all OFWs in the region, including Filipino seafarers. Strict implementation of safety protocols should be a priority in areas and countries considered high-risk areas.)

Tulfo, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Migrant Workers, likewise expressed his sadness over the incident and said his office is coordinating with the DMW to ensure the safety and welfare of the Filipino seafarers who survived.

“Sisikapin nating matiyak na sila ay ma-repatriate sa lalong madaling panahon at maibigay sa kanila ang lahat ng kinakailangang tulong, gayundin sa mga pamilya ng ating mga kababayang nasawi,” Tulfo said in a separate statement.
(We will work to ensure that they are repatriated as soon as possible and provided with all the necessary assistance, as well as the families of our fellow Filipinos who died.)

Tulfo also called on the DMW to ensure that manning agencies and shipping companies respect and enforce the seafarers’ “Right to Refuse Sailing” in high-risk areas such as the Strait of Hormuz without putting their entitlements and benefits at risk.
He said seafarers should also give informed consent and be properly briefed on the security risks before boarding and sailing.
Meanwhile, the DMW has likewise vowed support to the families and the colleagues affected by the incident, along with coordination with authorities.
The DMW also earlier said that it was arranging for the repatriation of the Filipino seafarers. /gsg

articles.title: Marcos orders aid for kin of PH seafarers killed in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered immediate assistance for the families of two Filipino seafarers who died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, Palace…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered immediate assistance for the families of two Filipino seafarers who died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Thursday.

Saudi Arabian shipping company Bari confirmed on Wednesday evening the deaths of the seafarers after its crude oil vessel SIDR was involved in a security incident before transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 31 at 11:40 a.m.

“Unang-una po nakikiramay po ang Pangulo at ang administrasyon sa pamilya ng dalawang seafarer mula sa Cabuyao, Laguna at Daanbantayan, Cebu. At nag-utos na po ang Pangulo, agad-agad na tulungan ang mga pamilya ng dalawa nating kababayan na nasawi at ibigay lahat ng kailangan nila pati ang benepisyo, compensation, insurance proceeds na naaangkop na dapat ibigay sa ating kababayan na nasawi,” said Castro at a briefing.

(First and foremost, the President and the administration extend their condolences to the families of the two seafarers from Cabuyao, Laguna, and Daanbantayan, Cebu. The President has also ordered immediate assistance for the families of our two fellow citizens who perished, as well as the provision of all necessary support—including the benefits, compensation, and insurance proceeds—rightfully due to them.)
“Hindi po pababayaan ng gobyerno, ng pamahalaan, ‘yung naiwan ng dalawa nating kababatan. Muli, nakikiramay po kami sa pamilya ng dalawa po nating sefarers,” she continued.
(The government will not neglect the families left behind by our two fellow citizens. Once again, we extend our condolences to the families of our two seafarers.)
According to Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac, the ship had 16 Filipino seafarers aboard when a fire broke out after projectiles hit.
The ship has since been grounded off the coast of Oman, where the Filipino seafarers, including the deceased, were disembarked, he said in an online presser.
He said the 14 other seafarers were unharmed, and the agency is arranging their repatriation. /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Four hours under the rubble, 97 years above it
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits.…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Guna Maya Bohara sometimes sings at night. It is the same bhajan—Hare Ram, Hare Krishna—that she used to sing during her stay at the elderly care home and during temple visits. Sometimes after singing, she asks a question: “Why did the water hit me?” The 97-year-old has asked the question more than once.

Apart from that, however, Bohara has mostly stopped speaking. Bohara is currently receiving treatment at Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. Her arms and legs have turned black and blue. She sometimes moves suddenly, almost involuntarily. She lies still for a while. Then another movement breaks the stillness. Doctors have diagnosed her with acute stress disorder.

On the morning of August 26, Bohara was in her room on the ground floor of the elderly care home at Devighat, a riverside town in Nuwakot. She was unaware that a glacier had collapsed high in the Himalayas. The collapse triggered a landslide, sending water and debris thundering down into the Trishuli River. The furious waters reached the ground floor, where Bohara was. It pushed her to the edge of the ground floor and left her there. The current was less intense on this side of the floor, witnesses say. Some of those caught in the current did not survive.

Nepal Police and Nepali Army personnel worked for about four hours to reach her, carefully clearing rubble carefully so as not to injure anyone still buried beneath it. Bohara’s relatives also rushed to the site. They brought a JCB excavator. With it, they worked together to move the debris away, inch by inch — moving, moving, moving, Dipak, Bohara’s great nephew, remembers, until there was space to lift her clear in its bucket.
Last Wednesday’s floods, however, were only the latest of Bohara’s ordeals in her long life.

At 97, Bohara has outlived her husband by 81 years. She was eight when she married him in Nuwakot’s Suryagadhi, at a time when child marriage was common practice. At 83, she chose on her own to move into a nursing home—Senior Citizens Welfare Foundation—in Devighat, close enough that her nieces could visit daily. She liked it there, among people her own age and looked forward to birthdays—her own and other residents—celebrated together.

By her twenties, she had already outlived nearly everyone who shared her blood: her husband, eight years into their marriage; both her parents, four years after that; her only brother, sometime later.
She never had children of her own.

What she had instead was her husband’s family, his three brothers, their wives, and in time their children. She raised thirteen nephews, twelve nieces as her own, sending every one of them to school, packing roasted maize for their lunch. Dipak says her family regards women of her generation as having quietly carried entire households through decades few now remember.
Bohara is the last of her generation left in the family.

Physically, she has proved more resilient than her age might lead one to expect. She has a pre-existing disability in her legs and an injury to her hand, caused by the torrents of water, is still being assessed, a CT scan and an X-ray pending. She survived on fruit juice for the first two days and has since moved to milk and full meals, Dipak said.

Of the people who share Guna Maya Bohara’s blood, none remain. Of the people who call her family, the nephews and nieces she once packed lunches for, there are twenty-five now, and they take turns at her bedside, waiting.

Dipak said that Bohara has not stopped asking, “Why did the water hit me?” He has tried to explain to her—more simply than what actually happened—that a lake, Gosaikunda, had burst far above them. She seems to understand, for a while. But hours later, she asks again: “Why did the water hit me?” /dl

articles.title: Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene
articles.summary:
Case is latest in string of post-Brexit deportations from country, which has been criticised for high refusal rate for British people to remain

The wife of a British man detained by police…

blocks.text: The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden.

Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks.
Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order.
“I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published.
“To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right.
“What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said.
Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010.
She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit.
A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit.

His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.”
During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September.
“They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am. They didn’t say anything about deportation or to bring passports.
“When we arrived they told us that they needed to talk to Charles privately, and after three hours they told me they were taking him to the detention centre and that they would deport him.
“I told them that they can’t do this because his case is in court and they have to wait for the outcome, but they told me they were going ahead,” said Lily.
She has pleaded with Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, to intervene.

“Why can’t Andy Burnham talk to the Swedish government? How many British families have to suffer in Sweden before Andy Burnham gets involved? How many families have to leave their homes, be forced into selling their houses?
“This is not humanity. This is not right. They should threaten the trade agreement,” she added.

Charles’s case comes amid growing controversy over Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement, which is supposed to have protected EU citizens in the UK and British citizens settled in the bloc before Brexit.
after newsletter promotion

Among those threatened with removal in the past month are 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old man in dementia care who has been in the country for 24 years.
A 34-year-old man revealed this week he was deported from Sweden in January despite having been in the country since he was 10 and being married to a Swedish woman in Gothenburg.
Two years ago another British woman, Kathleen Poole, was threatened with deportation because she had not provided financial statements to the Migration Agency while in full-time dementia care.

The Swedish migration minister defended the country’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement, saying the Migration Agency was following the rules and had granted a number of residency permits for Britons who had “reasonable grounds” for late applications.

However, concerns have been raised formally by the UK government through the EU-UK specialised committee, the official platform to raise issues over the working out of the Brexit deal, over the high number of late applications for post Brexit residency being rejected.

Sweden, along with 12 other EU member states, opted for a constitutive system requiring citizens to formally apply to extend their residency rights post Brexit. Others, like Spain, opted for a declaratory system requiring Britons to simply register their presence initially.
Lily says she and her husband phoned the authorities and used the correct form for residency and have been fighting ever since.
The latest statistics from the 2024 European Commission annual report show that 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency have been decided in Sweden.

According to analysis by the UK government, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, “a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3 and 4%”.

Sources added that this “constitutes 12% of all refusals across the EU member states, even though UK nationals in Sweden makes up only 1.55% of the total population of WA beneficiaries in EU member states”.
Denmark faced a similar controversy two years ago, but legislation was introduced to give British nationals a second chance to make the residency application.

articles.title: Filipinos’ visa-free stay in Thailand back to 30 days
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Thailand’s 60-day visa exemption will be replaced with 30-day visa free stays for tourists from 60 countries, including the Philippines, starting September 15, according to the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT).

“From 15 September 2026, travelers previously covered by the 60-day visa exemption will instead be subject to the applicable 30-day visa exemption, 15-day visa exemption, Visa on Arrival, or other relevant entry arrangements, depending on nationality,” the TAT said, citing the measure published in Thailand’s Royal Gazette on August 31.
The change effectively halves the visa-free period that Filipinos have enjoyed since Thailand expanded its visa-exemption policy in July 2024.
For most Filipino tourists, however, the change is unlikely to affect typical short trips, as stays of up to 30 days will remain visa-free.
From September 15, passport holders from the following 60 countries and territories may enter Thailand visa-free for tourism and stay up to 30 days:

Australia, Austria, Bahrain, Belgium, Bhutan, Brunei, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Fiji, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Maldives, Malta, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Oman, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Romania, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Taiwan, Turkey, Ukraine, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, and the United States.
TAT also explained that those using 30-day visa exemptions may enter through land-border immigration checkpoints no more than twice per calendar year. /dl

articles.title: Shopping to bar-hopping: USS Abraham Lincoln sailors unwind in Thailand after 250-day voyage
articles.summary: With military haircuts and moustaches, the US sailors stood out against the flip-flops of the usual Pattaya crowd, writes the BBC's Jonathan Head.

blocks.text: Night, though, is where this resort city comes into its own and puts on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars.

The few small establishments that makeup the heart of Pattaya's sex industry had been declared off-limits, a disappointment for the bikini-clad women packing the bars of Soi 6 who had been hoping for a windfall - from the sailors' nine months of unspent salary while at sea.
Conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, has impacted business in Pattaya, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.
But on Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to the sailors, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier.

By midnight some of the younger sailors there were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.
Conversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break.
"The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time", he said.

"It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long" he said.
Shakeira Fairfax, the mother of 25-year-old crew member Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low".
She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time.
"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.

The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US.

Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group.
It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.

US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".
US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".

articles.title: Coalition plan to cut tobacco excise by 80% ‘will kill people’ Labor says amid public health alarm
articles.summary:
Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan claim drastic cut to price of cigarettes and moves to legalise vapes will combat illicit tobacco trade

Leading public health experts, the Australian Medical…

blocks.text: Leading public health experts, the Australian Medical Association and Labor have rejected Angus Taylor’s plan to cut tobacco excise by 80%, labelling the move to curb soaring illegal cigarette sales as a backward step on tobacco control.

Taylor and Nationals leader Matt Canavan on Thursday announced plans for an 80% cut to excise, as well as moves to legalise and regulate vapes and nicotine pouches. The announcement comes weeks after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson proposed a 75% cut.

The opposition leader said the cut would reduce the excise on a standard packet of 20 cigarettes from about $30 to about $6, arguing it would undermine illicit tobacco dealers, who currently control more than half of all sales in Australia.
A Coalition government would spend $200 million on a law enforcement push against illicit sales, with increased funding for the Australian Border Force, federal police and other agencies.
“You don’t bring organised crime to its knees by protecting its business model,” Taylor said. “You have to destroy the business model, and that’s what the Coalition’s policy will do.”
Taylor said Parliamentary Budget Office modelling found the plan would add about $8 billion in revenue to the budget over four years, including from excise on pouches and vapes.
Labor has resisted calls to cut the excise rate, arguing there is no clear price point which would reverse the boom in black market sales.

World Health Organisation expert Benn McGrady said WHO recommends governments around the world raise taxes on tobacco products, and prices relative to real incomes, to ensure affordability is reduced over time. Reduced affordability reduces demand, lowering the burden of disease.
“Tobacco taxes are arguably the most effective measure to reduce demand for tobacco products and have played a key role globally in reducing smoking rates,” he said.
“From a public health perspective, taxes should be set with the aim of continually reducing affordability and demand.

“The global experience shows that strong tax administration and law enforcement are important components of tobacco taxation. These require a continued commitment from government and are the most important factor in ensuring compliance.”
Australian Medical Association president Danielle McMullen said the Coalition’s plan would undermine decades of public health efforts and even drive more Australians back to smoking.
“Making cigarettes more affordable is not the answer to tackling the illicit tobacco trade and would undermine Australia’s world leading public health efforts to reduce smoking,” McMullen said.
She said countries including Canada had seen an increase in smoking rates, including among young people, after excise cuts.

“Lower cigarette prices would likely increase smoking rates, particularly among price-sensitive groups such as young people and people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage, widening health inequities.”
Labor frontbencher Tanya Plibersek said the Coalition’s plan “will kill people”.
“We have some of the lowest smoking rates in the world because cigarettes are expensive,” she said.
“Tobacco is the only legal product that regularly kills two thirds of its regular users. If cars killed as many people as tobacco, people would be outraged about the road toll.
“This is a dangerous product and giving in to the bikies and the organised criminal gangs from overseas is not a solution to the illegal sale of these dangerous products.”

The Coalition’s plan was supported by economist Richard Holden, former deputy chief medical officer Nick Coatsworth and former Border Force official Rohan Pike. Pike has advised nicotine industry-linked organisations.
The trio wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Thursday, urging him to adopt the excise cut and warning increased accessibility of illegal cigarettes had undermined tobacco control strategies.

“The illicit market can only be driven out of the country by using overwhelming economic force, by further enhancing law enforcement, and by encouraging our smokers to the safer option of regulated vapes thereby reducing demand for tobacco,” they said.

articles.title: Channel smuggling gangs resort to 'mega-dinghies' as crackdown limits small boat supply
articles.summary: Once-rival criminal groups are being forced to work together because of a shortage of small boats, a BBC investigation has found.

blocks.text: A drop in small boats illegally reaching the UK is forcing people smuggling gangs to adopt new tactics, a BBC investigation has found.
And there are claims of more "mega-dinghies" being prepared, of the type seen arriving on UK shores in recent weeks.
The image of a 15-metre long small boat carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK drew condemnation from both newspapers and politicians.
Ministers were accused of "losing control" of illegal Channel crossings, and the French police again found themselves criticised for not intervening.

But evocative as the picture was, it also represented a new strategy by the increasingly frustrated people smugglers we encountered on France's northern shores - who attacked our crew with stones, and injured our cameraman.
They are running low on small boats, we have found. And once rival criminal groups are now having to work together by loading more migrants on fewer, larger vessels - just like the "mega dinghy".
The UK and France are announcing measures to increase the number of police officers on the French coast in order to try to stop the migrants.
The latest initiative comes as Andy Burnham prepares to host French President Emmanuel Macron at Downing Street for the first time since becoming prime minister.

Gang members have told our sources that others are being prepared, to the concern of emergency teams on both sides of the Channel, because of the increased risk to more lives. On 4 August 170 people had to be rescued after theirs caught fire in the middle of the Channel.

With French officers claiming they are now intercepting two-thirds of small boats before they can reach the coast, that means fewer crossing opportunities. And for those hoping to make the journey, it means a higher price.
Today, the gangs are quoting up to €2,000 (£1,700) per person. It used to be around €1,300 just a year ago. Their passengers also have to now pay in cash, to ensure commitment.
During one early low tide on Gravelines beach, we saw the only small boat to launch that day, and it was not what we expected.
At 09:30, a dozen or so migrants emerged from the sand dunes. Their distinctive orange life jackets, purchased from a local sports shop, made them easy to identify.
A need for speed at this point would be a fair assumption, but this was not to be the case. There was no running. It was almost orderly. A refined process where instructions were obeyed.

As they waded into the calm shallows of the Channel, their "taxi boat" came into view. It is simply a small boat that has departed from further along the coastline to avoid detection. Only now, they are being forced to set off from even greater distances. This one had left from Belgium.

The reason for the group not rushing was because the boat was already in the water. French police argue they are prevented from intervening at this point over fears of people drowning. It is to the long frustration of the British authorities, who would like their neighbours to at least adopt a more "case-by-case" approach.

As they clutch their phones in plastic wrapping, the group patiently waits for what they hope will be a voyage to a better life in the UK. Some tell me they are from Afghanistan. They are eager to catch their ride. Those who make it on are visibly elated.
After the last passenger, a young boy, is almost thrown on board, it inches out to sea, but it is not leaving yet.

At 09:49, another group of migrants move into the water and wait to be collected. An hour later, the boat indeed does return, but to another gathering that has emerged on a different part of the beach. A few run the vast distance across the sand to try to secure a spot. Most manage to clamber on.
As police officers watch from the shore, the small boat goes on to make five collections like this over three hours. The boarding becomes more frantic as the window of opportunity shrinks.
By 12:11, the small boat, with 82 people on board, finally moves off into the busiest shipping lane in the world. It is dwarfed by the passenger ferries in the background.
Everyone successfully made it to the UK. Small boats typically radio for help once they are in British waters, as the coastguard is compelled to rescue them and take them to shore.
What they leave behind in Gravelines is a scene of dejection and exhaustion. A limp toddler is carried past me towards a police officer, who revives him with a light shake.

This all unfolds next to four or so men casting their fishing rods into the increasingly choppy waters. It is peak holiday season here. They and other dogwalkers barely glance at the crestfallen migrants wading back to the stand.

Before, the gangs would often launch boats in the dead of night, but with increased police patrols, charity workers tell us the gangs now see the middle of the day as a better opportunity, as it takes taxi boats longer to arrive and it allows them to better co-ordinate boarding.

"You feel guilty being there - going to the beach and having a good time, while these families are in such terrible situations," observes a woman with her young daughter. They had been playing with a bucket and spade.
"It's hard," she admits. "We regularly see people on the beach attempting the crossing. It feels like living in two parallel worlds that have nothing to do with each other; it's really strange."

The migrants remaining will wait for their next opportunity, as per their agreement with the gangs. But because of more robust policing that wait is now typically weeks, even months, rather than days.
They also need a favourable weather window: the wind needs to ideally be under 5 knots and waves need to be less than 0.8m for a small boat to have a chance of making it across.

To improve their chances of avoiding detection and to be closer to a taxi boat, charity workers tell us migrants are also sleeping closer to the beach in the woods or among the dunes, instead of at the larger camps where they can wash, or receive food, water and medication.
It is after arriving at the largest settlement at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, that we soon find ourselves in direct confrontation with the people smugglers.

As the intense heat bears down on a tent where people can charge their devices, we initially meet two young Egyptian men who are visibly tired and disheartened. They have been staying in squalid conditions for months and have made several unsuccessful attempts to cross.
"The police stopped us from leaving and destroyed the boats," explains one. He says he wants to go to the UK so he can work and obtain legal papers.

A young Sudanese woman and Afghan man also told us they had also tried to cross dozens of times. We have been to the camp on several occasions over the past year, but this time there was a perceptible unease.

Riot police had cleared out the tents in the same week, and the day before around 400 migrants preparing for a taxi boat in the nearby Hardelot forest were forced to return after several fires broke out.
It is evident the migrants and the gangs have been repeatedly frustrated, and the sight of our camera in one corner of the camp leads to us being attacked.

After agreeing to stop filming, one smuggler, around 5'8" tall (172cm) and in a new grey tracksuit, tries to grab our camera. He then repeatedly throws rocks at us from close range, striking our cameraman above the eye.

articles.title: NBI probes Russian national over yacht documents in Samar
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has taken custody of a Russian national after authorities found inconsistencies in his documents and questioned the circumstances…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has taken custody of a Russian national after authorities found inconsistencies in his documents and questioned the circumstances surrounding his entry into the Philippines aboard a sailing yacht that had earlier encountered engine trouble off Samar.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said the yacht INGRID MARMARIS was towed on Aug. 29 to waters off Amandayehan, Basey, Samar, where its personnel and an NBI team inspected the vessel, its documents, and the Russian’s travel documents.
The yacht had earlier required assistance after experiencing engine trouble in waters off Marabut, Samar.
PCG search and rescue personnel aboard HSRB-031 began towing operations at about 7:30 a.m. on Aug. 29, bringing the vessel to the vicinity of Amandayehan.

At about 9 a.m., four NBI personnel from its Tacloban office arrived at the PCG motorpool area. The yacht, meanwhile, reached the area off Amandayehan at around 9:20 a.m., according to the PCG progress report.

About an hour later, PCG and NBI personnel boarded the yacht to inspect its documents, verify the identity and travel documents of its occupant, and examine other items relevant to the ongoing investigation.
During the inspection, the NBI team noted several inconsistencies and questionable circumstances in documents presented by Alexey Popov, a Russian national, according to the PCG.
The NBI also raised concerns over the circumstances of Popov’s entry into the Philippines, citing an apparent lack of appropriate documentation and/or authorization from relevant government agencies.
Popov was subsequently invited to proceed to the NBI office in Tacloban City for further investigation and verification.

At around 11:30 a.m., PCG and NBI personnel, together with Popov, left the yacht and proceeded to the NBI office. They arrived at about 12:05 p.m., where Popov was placed under NBI custody pending further investigation and coordination with other government agencies.
The PCG has taken custody of INGRID MARMARIS, which will be secured while the case is under evaluation.
The PCG said its personnel are continuing to coordinate with the NBI and other concerned agencies while maintaining the vessel’s security and preserving the investigation’s integrity./coa

articles.title: Russia to close branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut
articles.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced the move in statements carried by Russian newswires. It comes after Germany said it would close the Russian House in Berlin.

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut offers courses in German language and culture Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut would be closed on Russian territory.

Lavrov, in remarks carried by Russian news agencies TASS and Interfax, said Goethe-Institut locations would be closed in the Russian cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. The statement came after Germany said Russia was responsible for a ‌drone ⁠incident at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Germany's response included closing a Russian cultural center in Berlin and a Russian consulate in Bonn. On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the incident.

"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS. He added the centers had remained open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West."

Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union. In 2018, Russia ordered the closure of the British Council following a diplomatic dispute with the UK.
On Wednesday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said Moscow would retaliate "very soon" over Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn.

articles.title: Trump $1 coin makes him first living president on US currency in a century
articles.summary: The US Mint special edition is stamped with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST"

blocks.text: Donald Trump's portrait has made its way on to a US coin - the first time a living president has appeared on American currency in a century.
On Wednesday, the US Mint launched the $1 coin with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST", to celebrate America's 250th anniversary.
The special-edition coin captures "the spirit, pride, and legacy of a nation approaching its landmark anniversary", the US Mint said.

The coins - priced at $61 (£45) for a roll of 25 and $154.50 for a bag of 100 - were "not currently in stock" on the mint's website within hours of going on sale. The BBC has contacted the US Mint, the Treasury and the White House for further details.

The coin has been "created to celebrate this historic national milestone" with a "once-in-a-generation anniversary design destined to become a standout addition to modern collections", the US Mint said.
They are also being sold in vending machines at the US Mint store in Washington DC.
While the coins have a golden colour they do not contain any actual gold. According to the US Mint, they are 88.5% copper with the balance being made up of zinc, manganese and nickel.

blocks.text: AirAsia has signed its first-ever codeshare agreement, teaming up with Turkey’s largest low-cost carrier, Pegasus Airlines, to open seamless connections between Southeast Asia and Europe through Istanbul, the two airlines announced at AirAsia’s headquarters in Sepang, Malaysia, on Wednesday.

The partnership, unveiled before members of the media and witnessed by Turkey’s ambassador to Malaysia Nevzat Uyanık, will progressively open access to more than 100 routes between Asia and Europe, combining AirAsia’s Southeast Asian network with Pegasus’s reach across Europe from its hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport.

Five European destinations will be added from launch: Stansted (London), Vnukovo (Moscow), Esenboğa (Ankara), Zurich and Athens, all connecting through Kuala Lumpur and Istanbul. AirAsia will also lift its Kuala Lumpur–Istanbul frequency from four times weekly to daily by February 2027, up from the direct link AirAsia X has operated since November 2025.

blocks.caption: Farouk Kamal

blocks.text: Opening the event, Farouk Kamal, Deputy Group Chief Executive Officer of AirAsia Group Berhad, told guests the tie-up “marks the start of many more opportunities to come between the two airlines” and reaffirmed the group’s ambition to become the world’s first low-cost network carrier.
He said he had personally tried the product being announced on a trip last year and described the experience as “great” before handing over to colleagues to reveal the details on stage.

blocks.caption: AirAsia Seals First Codeshare With Pegasus, Bridges Asia and Europe

blocks.text: ‘Meaningful milestone’ in 25th year
In a statement accompanying the announcement, Bo Lingam, Group CEO of AirAsia Group, said the codeshare was a landmark moment as the airline marks its 25th anniversary.

“As AirAsia’s first-ever codeshare, this partnership marks a meaningful milestone in our 25th year and the next chapter in our evolution from a leading Asean low-cost carrier into a truly global travel network,” he said. “By connecting our extensive network across Asia with Pegasus’s strong European network from Istanbul, spanning 160 destinations across 56 countries, we are making Europe more accessible to our guests while creating a gateway for European travelers to discover Asean and beyond.”

blocks.caption: Elifnur Dogruoz

blocks.text: On stage representing Pegasus was Elifnur Dogruoz, the airline’s Group Head of Network Planning and Airline Collaborations, who told the audience the two carriers shared a common philosophy despite operating at opposite ends of Asia.

“At AirAsia your promise is ‘now everyone can fly.’ At Pegasus we say everyone has the right to fly – different words, but the same belief that air travel should be accessible for more people across more places,” she said, adding that Sabiha Gökçen was “more than a home” for Pegasus and a key gateway between Europe and Asia, just as Kuala Lumpur was for AirAsia.

blocks.caption: AirAsia Seals First Codeshare With Pegasus, Bridges Asia and Europe

blocks.text: She thanked Malaysia’s civil aviation authorities and airport operators for supporting the deal.
Pegasus chief executive Güliz Öztürk, who also did not attend the Kuala Lumpur event, added in a statement issued alongside the announcement:

“Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen is a natural connecting point between Europe and Asia. That AirAsia’s first-ever codeshare is with Pegasus Airlines is a source of pride: it reflects the network we have built from Istanbul over two decades and a hub that continues to grow. Our guests can now reach Kuala Lumpur seamlessly and, from there, AirAsia’s network of more than 140 destinations across Asia-Pacific.”

blocks.caption: Amanda Woo

blocks.text: Presenting the mechanics of the partnership to media, AirAsia’s Chief Commercial Officer, Amanda Woo, explained that travelers booking through AirAsia will receive both boarding passes at check-in, with baggage checked straight through to their final destination.

“One journey, one itinerary, a seamless experience,” she said, describing how a passenger flying from Kuala Lumpur to Athens via Istanbul would simply follow the signs to their next gate in Istanbul without needing to check in again or collect their bags.

Woo said the combined network would ultimately connect more than 100 routes between Asia and Europe and confirmed a further sweetener for early bookers: AirAsia will raise its Kuala Lumpur–Istanbul service from four times weekly to daily next year to meet expected demand.

The new connectivity also runs in reverse, with European travelers able to connect through Istanbul to Kuala Lumpur and onwards across AirAsia’s Fly-Thru network spanning Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, China, Vietnam and beyond. /dl

articles.title: Seven Thai airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports
articles.summary: BANGKOK — Passengers can check one 10kg box of fresh fruit for free at 20 Thai airports under a year-long scheme that began on September 1. Seven airlines will allow passengers to check up to…

blocks.text: BANGKOK — Passengers can check one 10kg box of fresh fruit for free at 20 Thai airports under a year-long scheme that began on September 1.
Seven airlines will allow passengers to check up to 10 kilograms of fresh fruit into the aircraft hold free of charge under a year-long program covering 20 airports across Thailand.

The Commerce Ministry, through the Department of Internal Trade, has signed a cooperation agreement with the Transport Ministry’s Department of Airports and seven airline partners: Thai Airways International, Thai AirAsia, Bangkok Airways, Nok Air, Thai Lion Air, Thai Vietjet Air and EZY Airlines.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: The program will run from September 1, 2026, to August 31, 2027, and is intended to help farmers distribute seasonal produce, encourage consumption of Thai fruit and support domestic tourism.

Banjongjitt Angsusingh, adviser to the commerce minister, said the government was seeking a wider range of distribution channels for agricultural produce entering the market. Her English name and title follow the Commerce Ministry’s official listing.

The cooperation would use the capabilities of airports and airlines to help travellers carry fruit home from producing areas and tourism destinations without having to pay additional transport charges, she said.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: One free 10kg box per passenger
Passengers using the service will be entitled to one standard fruit box with a maximum weight of 10kg.

The Department of Internal Trade will supply the boxes to participating airports from September 1. It will also work with provincial commerce offices to bring farmers into airport sales areas to sell seasonal fruit directly to travellers.
The Department of Airports will provide collection points for the boxes, assist passengers using the service and allocate temporary sales spaces for farmers at airports under its supervision.
The seven partner airlines will carry the fruit in their aircraft holds free of charge, subject to the 10kg limit per passenger, and promote the programme through their communication channels.
EZY Airlines is the official branding used by the participating Thai regional carrier.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: Twenty airports join pilot programme
The service will initially be available at airports in:

Nan, Lampang, Tak, Phitsanulok, Loei, Udon Thani, Khon Kaen, Sakon Nakhon, Nakhon Phanom, Roi Et, Ubon Ratchathani, Buri Ram, Prachuap Khiri Khan, Chumphon, Ranong, Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Krabi, Trang and Narathiwat.
Passengers should contact the designated service point at the airport to receive their fruit box before checking it into the hold.
The authorities initially aim to distribute 100,000 boxes, representing capacity for approximately 1,000 tonnes of fruit.

blocks.caption: Seven airlines offer free 10kg fruit check-in at 20 airports

blocks.text: Fresh fruit only, with strict packaging rules
Only fresh fruit will be accepted under the programme. The total weight must not exceed 10kg, and the fruit must be dry and free from moisture.

Passengers must use the official box supplied by the Department of Internal Trade at the airport service point. The container must be securely closed with adhesive tape or straps to prevent ants, insects and foreign objects from entering, as well as to stop liquid or odours from escaping.
Durian and other strongly scented fruit will not be accepted either in the cabin or as checked baggage because their smell could disturb other passengers.
“Before bringing fruit on a flight, passengers should ensure that it is packed properly,” Banjongjitt said.

“Durian and other strongly scented fruit must not be carried on board or placed in the aircraft hold, so that the smell does not disturb other passengers and everyone can enjoy a convenient and smooth journey.” /dl

articles.title: Another beluga whale sent from Marineland to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has died
articles.summary: Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says two whales have died after it took in several beluga whales from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont.

image.caption: A beluga whale swims in a tank at Marineland before being moved to an aquarium in the U.S. on Monday. Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says two whales, including one from Marineland, died today. (Carlos Osorio/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says two whales have died after it took in several beluga whales from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont.
Beluga was one of 2 that died at Shedd Aquarium Wednesday
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 02, 2026 10:48 PM EDT | Last Updated: 12 minutes ago
Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says two whales have died after it took in 10 beluga whales from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont.
Shedd says one whale, Rain, came from Marineland in mid-August while the other, Beethoven, was already a resident.
Marineland, along with Shedd and several other aquariums, recently completed an unprecedented relocation of captive whales after shipping 30 belugas and four dolphins to five destinations.
Another Marineland beluga, Peekachu, died last week after it became severely dehydrated.
Shedd says the deaths occurred Wednesday afternoon despite immediately trying to save the whales.
The aquarium says it does not know if the deaths are related, but they are performing tests and necropsies.

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada enters 'not guilty' plea in flood control-related plunder, graft charges
articles.summary: Sen. Jinggoy Estrada refused to enter a plea for his graft and plunder charges before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division on Thursday, September 3.

blocks.text: September 3, 2026 | 10:46am
Sen.Jinggoy Estrada leaves the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City after attending his scheduled arraignment on the graft case filed against him at the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026.
STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Jinggoy Estrada refused to enter a plea for his graft and plunder charges before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division on Thursday, September 3.
A "not guilty" plea was automatically entered on his behalf during his arraignment today.
Estrada is facing graft and plunder charges in connection to the alleged kickback scheme that led to irregularities in flood control works.
He is accused of receiving P573.75 million in kickbacks through the manipulation and rigging of processes and siphoning funds from the flood control budget.

Former Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Manuel Bonoan, originally charged alongside Estrada, has seen his charges dropped following a motion from the Ombudsman to have him be a state witness instead.
Estrada is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas and has been suspended from his work as senator.

articles.title: Two Filipino seafarers killed as Saudi tanker attacked in Hormuz
articles.summary: Fourteen other Filipino crew members aboard tanker Sidr are safe.

blocks.text: September 3, 2026 | 10:33am
The Strait of Hormuz as seen in this 2026 satellite imagery from NASA via Google Maps.
Philstar.com screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Two Filipino seafarers were killed after the Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker Sidr was struck by unidentified projectiles while approaching the Strait of Hormuz, the Department of Migrant Workers confirmed.
At an online briefing on Wednesday, September 2, Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said 16 Filipino seafarers were aboard the vessel when it was attacked late Aug. 31.
The strike caused a fire that the crew managed to contain, but two of the Filipino seafarers died.
The remains of the two victims have been taken to Oman, while the 14 surviving Filipino crew members are safe and being prepared for repatriation.
Cacdac said the Philippine Embassy and Migrant Workers Office in Oman are coordinating with Omani authorities to bring the crew members and the remains of those killed back to the Philippines.

Saudi national shipping company Bahri, which operates the Sidr, separately confirmed that two Filipino seafarers were killed in a "security incident" involving the tanker at around 11:40 p.m. local time on August 31.
High-risk waterway
The attack comes amid renewed fighting between the United States and Iran around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy shipping routes.

The United States struck Iranian missile launchers on Larak Island over the weekend, prompting Iran to retaliate against U.S. bases in Jordan. Maritime authorities subsequently reported attacks on commercial vessels transiting the strait.
Saudi Arabia has blamed Iran for the attack on the Sidr. Iran has not publicly accepted responsibility.
Cacdac said 31 vessels carrying 421 Filipino seafarers have been attacked in incidents involving the Strait of Hormuz since Feb. 28.
Of the 421 seafarers, 406 were unharmed, 10 were injured but have since recovered, three were killed and one remains missing. A total of 268 have returned to the Philippines.
Around 3,000 Filipino seafarers are still estimated to be aboard vessels in the wider Persian Gulf, according to the DMW.
Right to refuse
The DMW remains on red alert and has reminded shipowners to conduct risk assessments, put adequate security measures in place and avoid exposing Filipino crews to high-risk waters where possible.
Cacdac also reiterated that Filipino seafarers have the right to refuse to sail into designated high-risk or warlike areas.
"We are disallowing deployment to the extent that a seafarer exercises the right to refuse to sail. That right must be respected," Cacdac said.
The DMW and Bahri said assistance would be extended to the survivors and the families of the two seafarers who died. — with reports from Reuters

articles.title: Vietnam arrests deputy minister on bribery charge
articles.summary: HANOI — Vietnamese police arrested a deputy health minister on Wednesday for allegedly accepting huge bribes, part of a probe into a company accused of smuggling medical equipment, authorities…

blocks.text: HANOI — Vietnamese police arrested a deputy health minister on Wednesday for allegedly accepting huge bribes, part of a probe into a company accused of smuggling medical equipment, authorities said.
Communist Vietnam has pursued a high-profile anti-corruption campaign in recent years that has netted dozens of business leaders and senior government figures.

Deputy Health Minister Tran Van Thuan, a leading oncologist in Vietnam, was taken into custody “due to his acceptance of bribes involving a large sum of money”, the public security ministry said in a statement, without specifying the amount.
Thuan, 56, was appointed deputy health minister in 2020 and chairman of the National Medical Council in 2024.

His arrest came as part of a police investigation involving “smuggling” and “violations of accounting regulations causing serious consequences” at Viet My Medical Investment Joint Stock Company, the ministry’s statement said.

Police have arrested two executives and an accountant at the firm, which was allegedly set up to trade, resell and inflate the prices of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals before importing them from Singapore and Hong Kong into Vietnam, state media said.
Police also accuse company leaders of attempting to illegally import medical equipment.
AFP was unable to contact the company for comment.
Vietnam’s sweeping anti-corruption drive, accelerated by President To Lam, has removed many of his opponents, according to analysts, leaving him as the country’s most dominant leader in decades.
In May, former health minister Nguyen Thi Kim Tien was imprisoned for six years over her mismanagement of hospital projects, state media said.
Tien was rocked by corruption scandals in previous years, and was once voted the least popular official by lawmakers in the one-party state. /dl
