articles.title: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
articles.summary:
Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeking to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is ‘transformation’ of relations

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders.
“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.
Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.

“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.

The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.

The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.

“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.

The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”

Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.

Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.

On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.

The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.
“This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadet program members
articles.summary:
US defense secretary faced backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war

A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members…

blocks.text: A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.

On Monday night Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.

However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.

Its subjects are not members of Canada’s front-line military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.

The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.

Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to deescalate trade tensions.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.

David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.

The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement.
Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X.

“Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [make America great again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.”
Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”.

Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.”
The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.”

The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks.

On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after five people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country.

The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack.
Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”.
Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

articles.title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Germany
articles.summary: Russia is accused of growing increasingly reckless after Berlin blamed Russia for a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport.

blocks.text: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal".

"Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport.

"We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".
Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.
The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.
A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.
It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents.
The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.

Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.
Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil".
"We will not tolerate it," she said.

While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.
Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.
The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.

Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".
Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.

Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole.
"We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.
Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.
Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".

The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding from Kyiv to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.

She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine".

articles.title: Cops eye robbery in old American-Filipino couple’s slay in Dumaguete
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY— Police are investigating the shooting of an elderly American and his Filipino wife inside their home in Purok Katubhan, Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early Wednesday. Probers are…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY— Police are investigating the shooting of an elderly American and his Filipino wife inside their home in Purok Katubhan, Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early Wednesday.
Probers are looking into robbery as a possible motive.
The victims were identified as Mark Duell, 72, and Elsie Duell, 71, both of whom sustained gunshot wounds in an attack that occurred around 4 a.m., the police reported.
The Dumaguete City Police Station received a 911 call reporting the incident at approximately 6:08 a.m.
The couple’s 53-year-old stay-in caretaker told investigators that she woke up around 4 a.m. to find an unidentified male intruder inside the house.
The suspect was allegedly wearing a bonnet and carrying a firearm.
The helper reportedly said the gunman barged into the maid’s quarters and, at gunpoint, asked where the couple kept their money.
Authorities have requested the Scene of the Crime Operatives (SOCO) to study the crime scene.
Investigators led by PMSgt. Dell D. Anoos are finding out the full circumstances of the assault, identify the lone gunman, and determine the exact motive behind the crime. /apl

articles.title: 2 Filipino seafarers dead in Strait of Hormuz security incident
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Two Filipino seafarers have died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, a Saudi Arabian shipping company confirmed on Wednesday. According to Bahri, the shipping…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Two Filipino seafarers have died following a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, a Saudi Arabian shipping company confirmed on Wednesday.
According to Bahri, the shipping company, its vessel SIDR was caught up in a security incident while traversing the Strait of Hormuz on Sept. 1, at 4:40 a.m. (Philippine time).
“It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident,” the company said in a statement.
Bahri then vowed support to the families and the colleagues affected by the incident, and coordination with authorities.

“The safety and well-being in Bahri’s people remain its highest priority and the company remains committed to operating in accordance with the highest standards of safety, security and environmental protection,” Bahri added. /mr

articles.title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills five people at wedding
articles.summary:
Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities

Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five…

blocks.text: Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.

Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.

The US attacks on Tuesday ended a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.

Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devestating” retaliation.

Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.

“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.

In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.

Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate.”

It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.

The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.

Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
articles.summary: The Russian president wants to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's real intentions.

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.
"That's a secret. A military secret."
Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.
And that, I suspect, is the point.

Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.

It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".
Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.
We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.
But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.
Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".
Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?
Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.
So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.

"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."
Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.
The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.

For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.
Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.
"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.
Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".
"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.
He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.

"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."
There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.
Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?
There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.
But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

articles.title: Health chief awaits DOH bureau’s proposal on $10M PH pledge to WHO
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Health Secretary Edwin Mercado is expecting to receive a recommendation from his department’s Bureau of International Health Cooperation (BIHC) on its US$10 million pledge to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Health Secretary Edwin Mercado is expecting to receive a recommendation from his department’s Bureau of International Health Cooperation (BIHC) on its US$10 million pledge to the World Health Organization (WHO).

“The direction I gave is [to] focus first on local needs,” Mercado told lawmakers when asked by Iloilo 1st District Rep. Janette Garin at the House appropriations committee hearing on the DOH’s 2027 budget.
“We are waiting for the recommendation of the BIHC on how to move forward and also align with the directive that we will be focusing more on local needs,” he said.
The DOH made the $10-million pledge in 2024 to support WHO’s 14th General Program of Work, which is a “strategic document that sets a high-level roadmap and agenda for [its] work on global health.”
The pledge was set to be given to the WHO in tranches of US$2.5 million from 2025 to 2028.
Also at the hearing, Health Undersecretary and BIHC Director Maylene Beltran confirmed that half of the pledge, or US$5 million, had already been given to the WHO so far.
She justified the investment, saying “We do recognize that we need to also create our leadership in the international community.”
Upon questioning by Garin, Beltran committed to providing a list of how the US$5 million given to the international body had been spent.
“Perhaps, you can not spend that anymore and use it on your other needs,” Garin suggested, referring to the remaining amount in the pledge.
Beltran also confirmed that the DOH had proposed P167.2 million under its 2027 budget as part of the commitment to WHO.
Garin, a former health secretary, previously questioned the deal during the committee-level deliberations for the DOH budget last year.
She had asked then-Health Secretary Teodoro Herbosa whether he could realign the proposed funds for the pledge toward his department’s local projects.
Herbosa stepped down from his post last July. /apl

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
articles.summary:
Changes include fewer seats in parliament and new rules on presidential candidates ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding…

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

articles.title: Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Istanbul – maritime authorities
articles.summary: ISTANBUL — A cargo ship sank in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul after colliding with a second vessel, with rescuers hunting 10 people who were on board, Turkish officials said Wednesday. The…

blocks.text: ISTANBUL — A cargo ship sank in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul after colliding with a second vessel, with rescuers hunting 10 people who were on board, Turkish officials said Wednesday.

The incident occurred before dawn when the ALSU, an empty oil tanker, collided with the Tugberk Imamoglu, a cargo ship carrying rolled steel, which sank shortly after, the transport ministry’s maritime directorate said on X.
The collision occurred 18 nautical miles off Silivri district on the western edge of Istanbul province, the governor’s office said on X.
“Due to the Tugberk İmamoglu not responding to any calls and the crew not answering their mobile phones… it is believed the dry cargo ship has sunk,” the maritime directorate said.
The ALSU’s captain had reported the collision as happening at 3:15 am (0015 GMT), with 14 search and rescue vessels dispatched to the area backed by a helicopter, it said.
“Life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu which had 10 crew members on board, has been found at sea. Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside.”
The ALSU, which was damaged in the collision, was also joining in search and rescue efforts, it said.
At the time of the collision, the Tugberk Imamoglu was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled sheet metal, it said.
The maritime directorate initially said the ALSU was carrying 3,000 tonnes of motor oil, but later said the tanker was empty in a detail confirmed by the governorate.
The incident took place three days after deadly ferry accident off Northern Cyprus in which eight Turkish nationals died with rescuers still hunting for another 20 people listed as missing. /dl

articles.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
articles.summary: The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a…

image.caption: Kallas and other EU foreign ministers are in Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidencyImage: Ansgar Haase/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.
Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."
France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.
"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.
What has Germany said about its investigations?

Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.
Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

articles.title: Why do US troops have history with this Thai city?
articles.summary: The BBC’s Jonathan Head looks at the links between the US troops and the resort city of Pattaya as an aircraft carrier arrives nearby after 250 days at sea.

blocks.text: After a record 250 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand close to the city of Pattaya. Known for its raucous nightlife and sex tourism, the BBC's South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head explains the history between US troops and the beach resort.

articles.title: Congo’s Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
articles.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures. The…

blocks.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

“Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance,” DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.
“Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control,” he added.
Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.

“This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.
The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

“International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground,” Guterres said, warning that the world “must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference.”
Vaccination campaign gathers momentum
As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.
The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.

blocks.caption: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow

blocks.text: Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

“We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers,” he said on August 28.
Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

“It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type,” said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.
“Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well,” he added.
Communities seek protection
Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.
“I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination,” Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

blocks.caption: Health workers are worried about the spread of the virusImage: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Others are calling for wider access. “Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class,” said local resident Carine Lobwadji
Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

“I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid,” said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.
Violence hampers response
The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.
Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

“We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives,” Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.
Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.
Economic toll grows
Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.
Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.
Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

“In any case, it doesn’t work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical,” he said.
To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

“For us, it’s a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them,” Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

blocks.caption: Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washingImage: DW

blocks.text: Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

“We, the teachers, are ready, but we don’t have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem,” said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers’ inter-union alliance. “The first-grade children can’t read, nor do the parents. Several schools don’t have printers or computers. How will it go?”
Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

“It’s easy for me to understand when it’s my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don’t think it’s going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves,” said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children’s committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control. /dl

articles.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran’s fuel crisis
articles.summary: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country’s gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets. In cities across Iran, drivers…

blocks.text: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country’s gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations are closing before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say lines at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters (ca. 4 million gallons) a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.
Hours in line for a few liters
A resident of Karaj, a city west of the capital, Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around 5 liters (about 1.3 gallons).

“I’m in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far,” he said. “Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues.”
He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds, but again found a long line.
He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that could not be independently verified.
For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

“Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road,” one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.
Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.
For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.
Is Iran adulteratingits gasoline?
The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.
Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.
The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran’s refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.
Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements. But the timing has fueled public suspicion.
Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.
Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In the city of Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had been mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems.
Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.
Distrust over fuel quality grows
For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believed poor-quality gasoline had caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.
He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.
Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.
The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.
Tehran has argued that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.
But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.
Is a price increase in the works?
Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.
The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.
“Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers,” Mansour told DW.
But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour pointed to the financial condition of Iran’s oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.
When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argued, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.
Raising gasoline prices could, therefore, serve both as a demand management measure and a source of additional revenue.
A politically dangerous choice
The government has few easy options.
While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.
Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.
Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.
Today, the economic environment is considerably more fragile.
The war has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel lines are just another source of frustration.
For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.
But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control. /dl

articles.title: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?
articles.summary: There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to…

blocks.text: There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to receive an invitation.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, ​signed into force in early August, ​is intended to strengthen collective ​deterrence against any act of aggression. It stipulates that an ​armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded ​as an attack on all.
Some analysts believe the pact has already changed the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and South Asia.

“Although it is a collective defense understanding, from a strategic perspective it is primarily an initiative to maintain the regional balance of power and advance the respective interests of the participating states,” ​Navine Murshid, a political science and sociology professor at North South University in Dhaka, told DW.
Bangladesh govt. in favor of Mecca pact
Any move by Bangladesh to join, however, could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighboring India.
The two countries share a 4,096-kilometer (2,545-mile) land border, and have strong cultural and economic ties.
India, a fierce rival of Pakistan, sheltered many Bangladeshi refugees and provided military support to Bangladesh during its independence war against Islamabad in 1971.

However, ties between New Delhi and Dhaka have become increasingly contentious since a deadly student-led uprising in 2024 toppled then Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was considered a close ally of the Indian government.
Now living in exile in India, Hasina has since been convicted in absentia for crimes against humanity during the uprising. She has denied the charges.

blocks.caption: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?

blocks.text: Bangladesh’s current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement.
“We view this pact positively,” Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week.
But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members.
“If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively,” he said.
When asked about the remarks made by Bangladeshi officials, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation.

“We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India’s security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it,” Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India’s Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week.
Competing geopolitical interests
Analysts said Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact.

“The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars,” said Murshid.
“In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one’s position against the influence of other regional countries.”
Murshid added that Pakistan’s interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement “is driven by geographical and political considerations.”

“For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations,” she said, referring to India’s narrow land link to its northeastern states, which wraps around Bangladesh to the north. “If Pakistan’s defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships.”
In such circumstances, Bangladesh would have to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance, she explained.

“In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh’s role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan’s side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh’s capacity to manage,” she stressed.

Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. “Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day,” he told DW.

“They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance,” he added.
Would Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact?
Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needed to develop its own defense infrastructure and security systems sustainably.
She believes that becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka’s defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology.

“The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage,” she said.

However, Kabir fears joining the pact could limit Bangladesh’s geopolitical options and recommended a balanced approach. “We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration,” he said.
“Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests.” /dl

articles.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
articles.summary:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every…

blocks.text: Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

blocks.caption: Young farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
after newsletter promotion

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

articles.title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
articles.summary:
Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti

Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to…

blocks.text: Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.

He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks.

It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”.

Miliband has called plans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible.
Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK.
A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”.
Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine.

He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law.
“Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit.
“They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.”
Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention.

“The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide.
“But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.”

The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”
after newsletter promotion
Explaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.”
He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.”
Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical.

“They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.”

Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic.
“Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.”

Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us.
“We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”

articles.title: American, wife killed in Dumaguete City
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY—The police are investigating the violent killing of an American national and his Filipino wife in Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early on Wednesday. Capt. Stephen Polinar,…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY—The police are investigating the violent killing of an American national and his Filipino wife in Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early on Wednesday.

Capt. Stephen Polinar, spokesperson for the Negros Oriental Police Provincial Office, said the victims were shot at around 4 a.m. and were officially reported to the Dumaguete City Police Station around 6:08 a.m. Both victims were residents of the barangay.
Preliminary findings reveal that two unidentified male assailants carried out the attack before quickly fleeing the scene.
The Dumaguete City Police Station has since identified a person of interest in connection with the case.

While the primary motive behind the attack remains undetermined, law enforcement teams are actively conducting follow-up operations and gathering evidence to track down and apprehend the perpetrators./coa

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer

Drivers on residential roads in

blocks.text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.

The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.

Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.

“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: This is not standard flooding; it is Himalayan tsunami – Nepal minister
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign Affairs Minister Shisir Khanal speaks about the scale of the disaster, the logistical nightmare of high-altitude tunnel rescues, and why Nepal is shifting its diplomatic posture from requesting humanitarian aid to demanding climate compensation.
This Q&A has been edited for clarity and length, and is based on an interview on Kantipur TV’s Fireside by Rupesh Shrestha.
Minister, you recently returned from a field visit to Nuwakot. What is the real-world scale of this disaster?

When the first reports came in around 9am, our immediate conceptual imagery of a “flood” was a standard seasonal rise in river levels. But having spent the day in Nuwakot, I realized how limited our vocabulary is.

This was not a standard flood. With wave heights reaching 20 to 30 meters and speeds clocked at 180 kilometers per hour, this was a disaster of tornado-like velocity—what many are rightly calling a “Himalayan Tsunami”. It is a scale of disaster that is entirely outside the living memory of Nepal.

The damage is immense. Early assessments indicate that ten municipalities across Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Dhading—spanning 30 to 32 wards—have been heavily impacted, with additional damage downstream in Gorkha and Chitwan. We are looking at tens of thousands of damaged private homes, alongside heavily hit schools and multi-billion-rupee hydropower projects.
There has been criticism that the government was slow to seek international help, choosing instead to rely on its own resources. How do you respond to this?

There was absolutely no delay or rigidity on our part. The disaster unfolded rapidly. By 11am, while the floodwaters were still surging toward Dhading, the prime minister convened the National Disaster Council and mobilized security forces for immediate search and rescue.

Our initial priority was saving lives on the surface. By the second day, as our ground teams assessed the buried hydropower projects, they reported a critical need for highly specialized tunnel rescue support. We communicated this need immediately.

Because of high-altitude weather and transport limitations, airlift was the only viable option. Despite heavy cloud cover on the third afternoon that delayed flights, the Indian specialized tunnel rescue team arrived on the ground by the evening of the third day. The Chinese specialized team arrived by the afternoon of the fourth day, and a South Korean team is actively working at the Upper Trishuli site. Within 72 hours of identifying the need, international specialized rescue operations were fully operational on-site.
What is the status of the rescue operations at the buried hydropower tunnels, such as Trishuli 3A and Chilime? Is there still hope of finding survivors?

We must maintain hope and exhaust every possibility. Historically, there are global precedents—such as the 2018 Thailand cave rescue, or tunnel incidents in India in 2023 and China in 2021—where survivors were rescued after 14 to 18 days due to natural air pockets. Even if a tunnel is partially blocked, if there are air pockets, survival is possible.

However, the public must understand the extreme complexity on the ground. This is a highly complex disaster. These are not simple horizontal cave openings. The entire topography has shifted; hillsides have sheared off, leaving vertical cliffs covered in deep, unstable debris. In some areas, our rescue teams are literally sinking into quicksand-like mud.

At Trishuli 3A, teams had to locate the buried tunnel entrance using engineered maps because the surface construction was entirely erased. Instead of drilling horizontally, rescuers had to dig a vertical shaft—like a 30-foot well—just to reach the concrete crown of the tunnel. Once they breached it, they immediately began pumping in oxygen.

Currently, the Chinese team is working at the Trishuli 3A site, the Indian teams are deployed at Chilime and Langtang, and the South Korean team is coordinating at Upper Trishuli. While our security forces successfully cleared and entered the final points of the Rasuwagadhi tunnel on Monday, unfortunately, no survivors or bodies were recovered there. We are continuing to mobilise every local and international resource available.

The Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border is closed, and there are reports of temporary closures at Tatopani. How is the government managing bilateral trade and stranded travellers, particularly Mansarovar pilgrims?

Our northern supply chains and tourist corridors have been severely disrupted. Because the Tibet Autonomous Region is highly sensitive, Chinese regulations typically dictate that travelers must exit through the exact border post they entered.

To bypass this restriction, we actively negotiated with Chinese authorities to allow stranded Nepalis and foreign tourists to exit via alternative crossings. Stranded Nepalis have already begun returning through the Hilsa crossing in Humla. Furthermore, we have formally requested that the Korola border crossing in Mustang be used to evacuate foreign tourists who cannot return via Rasuwagadhi.

Regarding trade, hundreds of cargo trucks are currently stranded on the Chinese side of the Rasuwagadhi border. We have requested permission from Chinese authorities to reroute these cargo flows through the Tatopani and Korola crossings to prevent a total collapse of our northern supply lines.
You have stated that Nepal will no longer treat post-disaster assistance as mere “humanitarian aid” or bilateral grants. What is the government’s new diplomatic strategy?

Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.

We are shifting our diplomatic framework from “aid” to “justice and compensation”. This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability. The major industrial emitters—such as China, which is the world’s top emitter, the United States at number two, and India at number three—have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.

To this end, the Ministry of Finance has officially dispatched a formal climate compensation claim letter to our international partners. We will be raising this issue with absolute firmness and clarity at every upcoming international forum. This is a matter of civilizational survival. If our Himalayan glaciers disappear, the water security of over two billion people in South Asia—dependent on rivers like the Ganges and the Trishuli—will be permanently compromised. We are advocating not just for Nepal, but for the survival of South Asian civilization.

There is a strong perception that the government is more active on social media than on the ground, and that citizen deaths are treated merely as statistics. Why does Prime Minister Balendra Shah use his personal Facebook page to disseminate official government updates instead of official institutional channels?
